card.name: Richard Stallman
card.title: Founder of the GNU Project
card.knownFor: Advocate for free software movement
card.scouting: Richard Stallman is a pivotal figure in the free software movement. He advocates for user freedoms in software usage, study, and modification. His initiatives have shaped the landscape of software distribution and rights.
card.quote: Freedom is a matter of choice.

card.name: Linus Torvalds
card.title: Creator of the Linux Kernel
card.knownFor: Developing Linux and Git
card.scouting: Linus Torvalds revolutionizes software development with the Linux kernel and Git. His contributions foster a global open source community, driving innovation and collaboration across industries.
card.quote: Linus brings freedom and collaboration to software.

card.name: Aaron Swartz
card.title: Internet Activist and Programmer
card.knownFor: Contributions to RSS and Markdown
card.scouting: Aaron Swartz is a pivotal figure in internet activism and programming. He significantly contributed to various projects that shaped the web, advocating for open access and civic engagement. His legacy inspires many in the tech community.
card.quote: A prodigy who fought for freedom.

card.name: TJ Holowaychuk
card.title: Node.js Contributor
card.knownFor: Creator of popular Node.js modules
card.scouting: TJ Holowaychuk is a pivotal figure in the Node.js community, known for his innovative frameworks and modules. His work has significantly shaped web development practices and tools, making him a respected leader in open source.
card.quote: A master of Node.js frameworks.

card.name: Guido van Rossum
card.title: Creator of the Python Language
card.knownFor: Inventor of Python programming language
card.scouting: Guido van Rossum is a pivotal figure in programming, known for creating Python. His leadership as BDFL shaped the language's development and community, influencing countless developers worldwide.
card.quote: Guido's Python has empowered generations of coders.

card.name: Yukihiro Matsumoto
card.title: Creator of Ruby Programming Language
card.knownFor: Inventing the Ruby language
card.scouting: Yukihiro Matsumoto, known as Matz, is the creator of Ruby. He emphasizes simplicity and productivity in programming. His work inspires a vibrant community that values creativity and collaboration.
card.quote: Matz believes programming should be enjoyable.

card.name: Larry Wall
card.title: Creator of Perl Programming Language
card.knownFor: Inventing the Perl language
card.scouting: Larry Wall is a prominent figure in open source, known for creating Perl, a highly versatile programming language. His contributions to software development and community engagement have made a lasting impact on the tech landscape.
card.quote: Perl: The duct tape of the Internet.

card.name: Brendan Eich
card.title: Creator of JavaScript
card.knownFor: Co-founder of Mozilla and Firefox
card.scouting: Brendan Eich is a pivotal figure in web development, known for creating JavaScript. He co-founded Mozilla, championing open-source principles and fostering innovation in web browsers. His work continues to influence how we interact with the internet today.
card.quote: The man who brought interactivity to the web.

card.name: Rasmus Lerdorf
card.title: Creator of PHP
card.knownFor: Developing the PHP programming language
card.scouting: Rasmus Lerdorf is a pivotal figure in web development, best known for creating PHP. His work enables dynamic web applications and has influenced countless developers worldwide. He continues to advocate for open source principles.
card.quote: Rasmus Lerdorf transformed web programming forever.

card.name: David Heinemeier Hansson
card.title: Creator of Ruby on Rails
card.knownFor: Pioneering web application framework
card.scouting: David Heinemeier Hansson transforms web development with Ruby on Rails, emphasizing simplicity and productivity. As a co-founder of Basecamp, he champions remote work and efficient project management.
card.quote: Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication.

card.name: Ryan Dahl
card.title: Creator of Node.js
card.knownFor: Developing server-side JavaScript runtime
card.scouting: Ryan Dahl revolutionizes web development with Node.js, enabling JavaScript to run server-side. His work emphasizes efficiency and scalability, shaping modern web applications and influencing countless developers worldwide.
card.quote: Ryan Dahl turns JavaScript into a powerful server tool.

card.name: Evan You
card.title: Creator of Vue.js
card.knownFor: Developing the Vue.js framework
card.scouting: Evan You is a prominent figure in web development, known for creating Vue.js. His framework emphasizes simplicity and flexibility, making it popular among developers. He actively engages with the community, continuously enhancing the framework's capabilities.
card.quote: Evan's vision reshapes how we build interfaces.

card.name: Rich Harris
card.title: Creator of Svelte Framework
card.knownFor: Innovative JavaScript framework development
card.scouting: Rich Harris is a leading figure in modern web development. He creates tools that streamline coding processes and improve application performance. His work on Svelte revolutionizes how developers build user interfaces.
card.quote: Transforming the way we code for the web.

card.name: Jordan Walke
card.title: Creator of React
card.knownFor: Developing the React JavaScript library
card.scouting: Jordan Walke revolutionizes front-end development with React, a library that simplifies building user interfaces. His work emphasizes performance and usability, making it a favorite among developers worldwide.
card.quote: Transforming how we build user interfaces.

card.name: Dan Abramov
card.title: Co-Creator of Redux
card.knownFor: JavaScript libraries and tools
card.scouting: Dan Abramov is a leading figure in the JavaScript community, known for his work on Redux and Create React App. His contributions significantly enhance the development experience for React developers worldwide.
card.quote: Dan's tools empower developers to build better apps.

card.name: Sebastian McKenzie
card.title: Creator of Babel Compiler
card.knownFor: JavaScript transpiler development
card.scouting: Sebastian McKenzie is a pivotal figure in JavaScript development. He creates Babel, a tool that allows developers to use the latest JavaScript features while ensuring compatibility with older browsers.
card.quote: Babel: bridging the gap in JavaScript.

card.name: Isaac Z. Schlueter
card.title: Node.js Package Manager Creator
card.knownFor: Founder of npm, Inc.
card.scouting: Isaac Z. Schlueter revolutionizes JavaScript development with npm, the world's largest software registry. His work fosters collaboration and innovation, making it easier for developers to share and reuse code.
card.quote: Empowering developers, one package at a time.

card.name: Matt Mullenweg
card.title: Co-founder of WordPress
card.knownFor: Leading the WordPress project
card.scouting: Matt Mullenweg is a key figure in web development, known for co-founding WordPress. He champions open-source principles and has significantly influenced online publishing and content management systems.
card.quote: Empowering creators through open-source innovation.

card.name: Dries Buytaert
card.title: Creator of Drupal
card.knownFor: Founding the Drupal content management system
card.scouting: Dries Buytaert is a pivotal figure in open source, known for creating Drupal, a leading content management system. He champions community-driven development and continues to influence the web landscape through his work at Acquia.
card.quote: Empowering the web, one site at a time.

card.name: Brian Behlendorf
card.title: Co-founder of Apache Software Foundation
card.knownFor: Leading the Apache HTTP Server project
card.scouting: Brian Behlendorf is a pivotal figure in open source, known for co-founding the Apache Software Foundation. His leadership in developing the Apache HTTP Server has significantly shaped the web landscape, promoting collaboration and innovation in software development.
card.quote: Brian champions the spirit of open collaboration.

card.name: Roy Fielding
card.title: Architect of REST
card.knownFor: Founding the REST architectural style
card.scouting: Roy Fielding is a pivotal figure in web architecture, known for his creation of REST. His work on HTTP and the Apache HTTP Server has profoundly influenced how modern web applications are designed and interact.
card.quote: Fielding's REST principles revolutionized web communication.

card.name: Eric S. Raymond
card.title: Open Source Advocate
card.knownFor: Author of 'The Cathedral and the Bazaar'
card.scouting: Eric S. Raymond is a prominent figure in the open source movement. He advocates for transparency in software development and has authored influential works that shape modern programming practices.
card.quote: Raymond's insights revolutionized software development.

card.name: Bruce Perens
card.title: Co-founder of Open Source Initiative
card.knownFor: Advocate for open source software
card.scouting: Bruce Perens is a pivotal figure in the open source movement. He co-founded the Open Source Initiative and authored the Open Source Definition, which shapes software licensing today. His advocacy continues to influence software development worldwide.
card.quote: Open source is a philosophy, not just a license.

card.name: Ian Murdock
card.title: Founder of Debian Project
card.knownFor: Creating the Debian Linux distribution
card.scouting: Ian Murdock is a pivotal figure in open source, known for founding the Debian Project. His vision for a collaborative operating system has influenced countless distributions and fostered a strong community ethos.
card.quote: Debian: a legacy of freedom and collaboration.

card.name: Mark Shuttleworth
card.title: Founder of Ubuntu
card.knownFor: Creating the Ubuntu operating system
card.scouting: Mark Shuttleworth is a visionary entrepreneur and philanthropist. He founded Ubuntu, which revolutionized Linux accessibility. His commitment to open source fosters innovation and community engagement worldwide.
card.quote: Shuttleworth believes in the power of freedom through software.

card.name: Theo de Raadt
card.title: Founder of OpenBSD
card.knownFor: Advocate for open-source security
card.scouting: Theo de Raadt leads the OpenBSD project, emphasizing security and code correctness. His work on OpenSSH has transformed secure communications globally. He is a prominent figure in the open-source community.
card.quote: Security and simplicity define his legacy.

card.name: D. Richard Hipp
card.title: Creator of SQLite
card.knownFor: Developing the SQLite database
card.scouting: D. Richard Hipp is a prominent software developer known for creating SQLite, a lightweight database widely used in applications. His work on Fossil and Tcl further showcases his versatility and impact in the open-source community.
card.quote: SQLite: the database that fits everywhere.

card.name: Fabrice Bellard
card.title: Creator of QEMU
card.knownFor: Contributions to emulation and programming languages
card.scouting: Fabrice Bellard is a prominent figure in open source software, known for his groundbreaking work in emulation and programming languages. His projects, especially QEMU and FFmpeg, have significantly influenced the tech landscape.
card.quote: A pioneer in emulation and multimedia.

card.name: Andrew Tridgell
card.title: Creator of Samba
card.knownFor: Pioneering open-source file sharing
card.scouting: Andrew Tridgell is a key figure in open-source software, known for creating Samba and rsync. His work enables seamless file sharing across different operating systems, making him a vital contributor to the open-source community.
card.quote: Tridgell bridges systems with open-source innovation.

card.name: Bram Moolenaar
card.title: Creator of Vim Editor
card.knownFor: Developing the Vim text editor
card.scouting: Bram Moolenaar is a prominent figure in software development, known for creating Vim, a highly configurable text editor. His work emphasizes efficiency and productivity, making Vim a staple among programmers worldwide.
card.quote: Vim: The editor that keeps on giving.

card.name: Brian Fox
card.title: Co-Creator of GNU Bash
card.knownFor: Developing the Bourne Again Shell
card.scouting: Brian Fox is a pivotal figure in the open source community, known for creating GNU Bash, a widely used command-line shell. His work has significantly influenced the development of free software and the GNU Project, promoting software freedom.
card.quote: Brian Fox's legacy lives on in every terminal.

card.name: Werner Koch
card.title: Principal Author of GnuPG
card.knownFor: Creating the GNU Privacy Guard
card.scouting: Werner Koch is a pivotal figure in free software, known for his work on GnuPG. His contributions enhance digital security and privacy for users worldwide. He actively promotes free software principles through his leadership roles.
card.quote: Koch champions freedom in digital security.

card.name: Miguel de Icaza
card.title: Creator of GNOME and Mono
card.knownFor: Pioneering free software development
card.scouting: Miguel de Icaza is a key figure in free software, driving innovation with GNOME and Mono. His work empowers developers and enhances user experiences across platforms.
card.quote: A true champion of open source software.

card.name: Federico Mena Quintero
card.title: Co-Creator of GNOME
card.knownFor: Developing the GNOME desktop environment
card.scouting: Federico Mena Quintero is a pivotal figure in open-source software, known for co-creating the GNOME desktop environment. His work enhances user experience across various Linux distributions, making technology accessible and user-friendly.
card.quote: Transforming the Linux desktop experience.

card.name: Havoc Pennington
card.title: Pioneer of Desktop Environments
card.knownFor: Contributions to GNOME and D-Bus
card.scouting: Havoc Pennington drives innovation in desktop environments, enhancing user experience with GNOME and D-Bus. His work supports seamless communication between applications, making software more accessible and efficient.
card.quote: A key figure in the free software movement.

card.name: Keith Packard
card.title: X Window System Developer
card.knownFor: Pioneering work on graphical interfaces
card.scouting: Keith Packard is a prominent software developer recognized for his significant contributions to the X Window System, which revolutionized graphical interfaces in computing. His work continues to impact open source software development today.
card.quote: A pioneer in graphical interface innovation.

card.name: Lennart Poettering
card.title: Systemd Creator
card.knownFor: Developing systemd and related technologies
card.scouting: Lennart Poettering is a pivotal figure in modern Linux systems. He revolutionizes how services are managed with systemd, impacting boot processes and service management across distributions. His work on audio and service discovery further enhances user experience.
card.quote: Revolutionizing Linux with innovative technologies.

card.name: Greg Kroah-Hartman
card.title: Linux Kernel Maintainer
card.knownFor: Leading Linux kernel development
card.scouting: Greg Kroah-Hartman is a pivotal figure in Linux kernel development, ensuring its stability and performance. His work on driver backports and Ksplice enhances system reliability, making him a respected leader in the open source community.
card.quote: A guardian of the Linux kernel.

card.name: Alan Cox
card.title: Linux Kernel Developer
card.knownFor: Contributions to the Linux kernel
card.scouting: Alan Cox is a prominent figure in the Linux community, known for his extensive contributions to the Linux kernel. He plays a crucial role in maintaining kernel releases and enhancing networking capabilities, solidifying his legacy in open source software.
card.quote: A key architect of Linux's evolution.

card.name: Chris Lattner
card.title: Creator of LLVM
card.knownFor: Developing the LLVM compiler infrastructure
card.scouting: Chris Lattner is a pivotal figure in programming language design and compiler technology. His work on LLVM revolutionizes how software is compiled, while Swift has transformed iOS development, making it more accessible and efficient.
card.quote: A visionary in compilers and programming languages.

card.name: Graydon Hoare
card.title: Creator of the Rust Language
card.knownFor: Developing the Rust programming language
card.scouting: Graydon Hoare is a prominent software engineer known for creating Rust. His work emphasizes safety and concurrency, making a significant impact on modern programming practices. He continues to influence the open source community.
card.quote: Graydon's vision redefines how we think about safety in programming.

card.name: Steve Klabnik
card.title: Open Source Advocate
card.knownFor: Contributions to Rust programming language
card.scouting: Steve Klabnik is a prominent figure in the Rust community, known for his advocacy of open source software. He plays a crucial role in enhancing Rust's documentation and fostering a welcoming environment for developers.
card.quote: Steve champions the spirit of open source.

card.name: Salvatore Sanfilippo
card.title: Creator of Redis
card.knownFor: Developing the Redis database
card.scouting: Salvatore Sanfilippo, known as antirez, is the creator of Redis, a powerful in-memory data structure store. His work has revolutionized data handling and caching in modern applications, making him a key figure in open source software.
card.quote: Redis: Fast, reliable, and open source.

card.name: Michael Widenius
card.title: Creator of MySQL Database
card.knownFor: Co-founder of MySQL AB
card.scouting: Michael 'Monty' Widenius revolutionizes data management with MySQL, a leading open-source database. His commitment to community-driven development continues through MariaDB, ensuring robust alternatives in database technology.
card.quote: Monty believes in open-source freedom.

card.name: Brad Fitzpatrick
card.title: Creator of LiveJournal
card.knownFor: Pioneering social networking platform
card.scouting: Brad Fitzpatrick is a key figure in social networking and open source. He creates impactful projects like LiveJournal and Memcached, which have influenced web development and community building.
card.quote: Innovator of social platforms and caching solutions.

card.name: Solomon Hykes
card.title: Creator of Docker
card.knownFor: Pioneering container technology
card.scouting: Solomon Hykes revolutionizes software deployment with Docker, enabling developers to create, deploy, and manage applications in containers. His work fosters innovation in cloud computing and microservices, making it easier for teams to collaborate and scale.
card.quote: Hykes transforms how we think about applications.

card.name: Mitchell Hashimoto
card.title: Co-founder of HashiCorp
card.knownFor: Infrastructure automation software
card.scouting: Mitchell Hashimoto is a leading figure in infrastructure automation. He co-founds HashiCorp and creates tools that simplify cloud management. His work empowers developers to streamline workflows and enhance productivity.
card.quote: Transforming infrastructure management, one tool at a time.

card.name: Kevin Mitnick
card.title: The World’s Most Wanted Hacker
card.knownFor: Social engineering, and the manhunt that followed it
card.scouting: Talked his way into more networks than he ever broke into. A teenage phone phreak who became the FBI’s most-wanted hacker, was captured in 1995, served five years, and came out the other side as a security consultant and author of The Art of Deception. He made the industry admit the obvious: the person on the phone is the vulnerability.
card.note: The card that defines the set. Nobody argues about this one.

sources.label: Takedown — the 1995 arrest, as told by Markoff and Shimomura

card.name: John Draper
card.title: The Original Phone Phreak
card.knownFor: The 2600 Hz whistle that opened the phone network
card.scouting: Discovered that a toy whistle packed in a cereal box produced the exact 2600 Hz tone AT&T used to signal a free trunk line. The blue-box scene that grew from it pulled in two young Californians named Wozniak and Jobs, and drew the blueprint for every generation of hacker that followed.
card.note: Patient zero for hacker culture. The whistle is the artifact of the century.

sources.label: Blue box — the 2600 Hz signalling exploit

card.name: Robert Tappan Morris
card.title: Author of the Morris Worm
card.knownFor: The 1988 worm that took down the early internet
card.scouting: Released a self-replicating program from MIT in November 1988 that reinfected hosts far faster than intended and knocked out a large share of the machines on the internet. First person convicted under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. Went on to become an MIT professor and a co-founder of Y Combinator.
card.note: The accident that created the entire incident-response industry — CERT exists because of this.

sources.label: United States v. Morris (1991) — the first CFAA conviction

card.name: Peiter Zatko
card.title: L0pht Elder, Government Insider
card.knownFor: Telling the Senate he could take down the internet in 30 minutes
card.scouting: Front man of L0pht Heavy Industries and co-author of L0phtCrack. In 1998 the crew testified before the US Senate under their handles and warned that the internet could be taken down in half an hour. Later ran cyber programs at DARPA, worked security at Google and Stripe, and blew the whistle on Twitter’s security posture in 2022.
card.note: The rare legend who went from underground to the Senate floor without changing his story.

card.name: Kevin Poulsen
card.title: The Phreak Who Won a Porsche
card.knownFor: Taking over LA phone lines to win a radio contest
card.scouting: Seized control of every telephone line into KIIS-FM to guarantee he was caller 102 and won a Porsche. Ran from the FBI, was profiled on Unsolved Mysteries, and served time. Reinvented himself as an investigative journalist at Wired and helped build SecureDrop, the whistleblower system used by newsrooms worldwide.
card.note: Rigged a radio contest, then spent his second act protecting sources.

card.name: Eric Corley
card.title: Publisher of 2600
card.knownFor: 2600: The Hacker Quarterly and Off The Hook
card.scouting: Founded 2600: The Hacker Quarterly in 1984 and has been broadcasting Off The Hook on WBAI since 1988. Organizer of the HOPE conferences and a defendant in the DeCSS case, where the courts first wrestled with whether publishing code is speech.
card.note: The set needs a printing press, and this is it.

card.name: Loyd Blankenship
card.title: Author of the Hacker Manifesto
card.knownFor: “The Conscience of a Hacker,” written after his arrest
card.scouting: Member of the Legion of Doom who, hours after being arrested in 1986, wrote the essay that Phrack published as The Conscience of a Hacker. Later wrote GURPS Cyberpunk for Steve Jackson Games — the manuscript the Secret Service seized in a raid that helped spark the founding of the EFF.
card.note: One page of text that every hacker under thirty could still quote a decade later.

sources.label: “The Conscience of a Hacker”, Phrack vol. 1 no. 7

card.name: Jeff Moss
card.title: Founder of DEF CON
card.knownFor: Building the conferences where the scene meets
card.scouting: Threw a going-away party for a friend in Las Vegas in 1993 and accidentally founded DEF CON, now the largest hacker gathering on earth. Also founded Black Hat, served on the US Homeland Security Advisory Council, and spent years translating between the underground and the institutions that fear it.
card.note: Every other legend in this set has stood on a stage he built.

card.name: Dan Kaminsky
card.title: The Man Who Patched DNS
card.knownFor: The 2008 DNS cache-poisoning flaw
card.scouting: Found a flaw that let an attacker poison DNS caches and quietly redirect any name on the internet. Instead of publishing, he organized a secret multi-vendor patch effort and got the whole internet fixed on one coordinated day in July 2008. Died in 2021 at 42, and the industry has not stopped talking about him since.
card.note: Proof that the biggest bug of your career is a responsibility, not a trophy.

sources.label: Wired, 2008 — how Kaminsky found the flaw

card.name: Clifford Stoll
card.title: The Astronomer Who Caught a Spy
card.knownFor: The Cuckoo’s Egg
card.scouting: Chased a 75-cent accounting error at Lawrence Berkeley Lab all the way to Markus Hess, a West German hacker selling US military data to the KGB. His logbooks and homemade tripwires invented network intrusion detection by hand, and The Cuckoo’s Egg is still the best on-ramp anyone ever wrote.
card.note: The first documented cyber-espionage case, solved by an astronomer with a printer.

card.name: Tsutomu Shimomura
card.title: The Man Who Tracked Mitnick
card.knownFor: The 1995 pursuit and TCP sequence-prediction analysis
card.scouting: Computational physicist at San Diego Supercomputer Center whose own machines were broken into on Christmas Day 1994. His analysis of the IP-spoofing and TCP sequence-prediction attack, and the cell-tracking work that followed, led federal agents to Kevin Mitnick in Raleigh in February 1995.
card.note: Card 1’s opposite number. They belong in the same pack.

sources.label: IP address spoofing — the technique used against him

card.name: Mark Abene
card.title: Masters of Deception
card.knownFor: The MOD-versus-LOD hacker war
card.scouting: Teenage authority on telephone switching systems and the public face of Masters of Deception. His 1994 prison sentence was widely read as a message being sent to a whole generation; New York magazine had already named him one of the city’s smartest people.
card.note: The last of the pure telephone hackers before the internet took over.

card.name: Susan Headley
card.title: Early Social Engineer
card.knownFor: Talking her way into military and telco systems
card.scouting: Ran in the same Los Angeles phreaking circles as Mitnick and Lewis De Payne and specialized in the human layer — pretext calls, trashed printouts, borrowed credentials. One of the very few women documented in the earliest scene, and she walked away from it entirely.
card.note: Written out of most retellings. This set puts her back in.

card.name: Adrian Lamo
card.title: Intruder, Then Informant
card.knownFor: The New York Times intrusion, and reporting Chelsea Manning
card.scouting: Broke into Microsoft, Yahoo and The New York Times from library terminals and coffee shops, usually telling the victim afterwards. In 2010 he reported Chelsea Manning to the authorities after she confided in him — a decision that split the community permanently. Died in 2018.
card.note: The most divisive card in the set, and it stays in. The history is the history.

card.name: Gary McKinnon
card.title: The UFO Hunter
card.knownFor: Searching US military networks for evidence of UFOs
card.scouting: Scanned US military and NASA networks for machines with blank administrator passwords and found plenty. US prosecutors called it the biggest military computer hack of all time; a decade-long extradition fight ended in 2012 when the UK Home Secretary blocked it on human-rights grounds.
card.note: Two words: no password. That is the whole exploit.

sources.label: BBC, 2012 — extradition to the US blocked

card.name: Jonathan James
card.title: The Teenager Who Got NASA’s Source
card.knownFor: First juvenile jailed in the US for computer crime
card.scouting: At fifteen, installed a backdoor on a Defense Threat Reduction Agency server and downloaded NASA software supporting the International Space Station. Sentenced in 2000 as the first juvenile incarcerated for cybercrime in the US. Died by suicide in 2008 while under investigation in an unrelated case he denied any part in.
card.note: A cautionary card. The set tells it straight or not at all.

card.name: Chris Wysopal
card.title: Architect of Responsible Disclosure
card.knownFor: L0pht, the Senate testimony, and disclosure norms
card.scouting: One of the seven L0pht members who testified to the Senate in 1998. Spent the following decades turning ad-hoc bug reporting into a process the industry could live with, then co-founded Veracode to make application security something you can actually buy.
card.note: Half the reason a vendor takes your bug report seriously today.

card.name: Katie Moussouris
card.title: The Bug Bounty Builder
card.knownFor: Microsoft’s first bounty program and Hack the Pentagon
card.scouting: Created Microsoft’s first bug bounty program, then ran Hack the Pentagon, the first bounty program in the history of the US federal government. Fought to keep defensive research from being criminalized under the Wassenaar Arrangement, and founded Luta Security.
card.note: Turned “we do not pay for bugs” into an industry standard line item.

card.name: Joanna Rutkowska
card.title: Blue Pill
card.knownFor: Hypervisor rootkits and Qubes OS
card.scouting: Presented Blue Pill at Black Hat 2006, a rootkit that moved a running OS into a hypervisor beneath it, and coined the Evil Maid attack for machines left unattended. Then built the answer: Qubes OS, a desktop that assumes compromise and isolates by compartment.
card.note: Broke the platform, then shipped a better one. Very few do both.

card.name: Michał Zalewski
card.title: The Fuzzer
card.knownFor: american fuzzy lop and Silence on the Wire
card.scouting: Wrote afl, the coverage-guided fuzzer that found thousands of bugs across the software everyone depends on and reset the state of the art for everyone else. Author of Silence on the Wire and The Tangled Web, and a long-time browser security lead at Google.
card.note: The bug-finding tool with the highest body count in open source history.

card.name: Alexander Peslyak
card.title: John the Ripper
card.knownFor: Password cracking and Linux hardening
card.scouting: Wrote John the Ripper, still the reference password cracker three decades on. Founded Openwall, pioneered non-executable stack patches for Linux, published early return-into-libc work, and runs the oss-security list where the industry argues about disclosure in public.
card.note: Runs the mailing list where your favorite CVE was first announced.

sources.label: oss-security, the disclosure list he runs

card.name: HD Moore
card.title: Creator of Metasploit
card.knownFor: Making exploitation a framework, not a one-off
card.scouting: Released Metasploit in 2003 and turned exploit development from scattered one-off code into a shared, modular framework every penetration tester now learns first. Later ran internet-wide scanning projects that mapped just how much of the internet is quietly exposed.
card.note: Changed what a working exploit is worth by making them all free.

card.name: Barnaby Jack
card.title: ATM Jackpotting
card.knownFor: Making cash machines spit money on stage
card.scouting: Walked onto the Black Hat 2010 stage, ran his Jackpotting demo, and made two ATMs pour out cash in front of the room. Then turned to insulin pumps and pacemakers, showing that implanted medical devices could be attacked wirelessly. Died in 2013, days before he was due to present that research.
card.note: The most theatrical demo in the history of the conference circuit.

card.name: Charlie Miller
card.title: The Car Hacker
card.knownFor: Remotely killing a Jeep on the highway
card.scouting: Won Pwn2Own repeatedly, was the first to publicly exploit the iPhone, and then, with Chris Valasek, cut the transmission of a Jeep Cherokee on a live highway from a couch miles away. Chrysler recalled 1.4 million vehicles. Automotive security became a real discipline overnight.
card.note: One demo, 1.4 million recalled vehicles. Hard to argue with the receipts.

sources.label: Wired, 2015 — hackers remotely kill a Jeep on the highway

card.name: Chris Valasek
card.title: CAN Bus Whisperer
card.knownFor: The Jeep hack, with Charlie Miller
card.scouting: Reverse-engineered the internal networks of production vehicles and, with Miller, demonstrated full remote control of a Jeep Cherokee in 2015. Both went on to build security teams inside the autonomous-vehicle industry they had just put on notice.
card.note: Ships as a pair card with 24. Collectors will want both.

sources.label: Wired, 2015 — hackers remotely kill a Jeep on the highway
“Remote Exploitation of an Unaltered Passenger Vehicle” (PDF)

card.name: Samy Kamkar
card.title: The Worm That Ate MySpace
card.knownFor: The Samy worm, and a decade of hardware hacks
card.scouting: Released a self-propagating cross-site scripting worm in 2005 that added over a million MySpace friends in under a day and took the site down. After his sentence he kept publishing: SkyJack, OwnStar, KeySweeper, and a long line of garage-door and car-key radio attacks explained on video for anyone.
card.note: The best explainer in the game. Half the set learned from his videos.

sources.label: Kamkar’s own writeup of the MySpace worm

card.name: George Hotz
card.title: Jailbreaker
card.knownFor: Unlocking the first iPhone and cracking the PS3
card.scouting: At seventeen, unlocked the original iPhone from its carrier. Then published PlayStation 3 root keys and was sued by Sony, in a case that became a rallying point for the right to modify hardware you own. Later founded comma.ai and worked on open self-driving.
card.note: The card about who actually owns the device in your pocket.

sources.label: Sony Computer Entertainment America v. Hotz

card.name: Marcus Hutchins
card.title: The WannaCry Killswitch
card.knownFor: Stopping a global ransomware outbreak for $10.69
card.scouting: Reversing WannaCry as it tore through hospitals in May 2017, he spotted an unregistered domain in the code and bought it, unintentionally triggering the killswitch that halted the outbreak. Arrested months later over earlier banking-malware code he had written as a teenager; he pled guilty, was sentenced to time served, and now works in threat research.
card.note: Saved the NHS on a Friday and was arrested by August. Both halves are the card.

sources.label: Wired — The Confessions of Marcus Hutchins

card.name: Karsten Nohl
card.title: Breaker of Radios
card.knownFor: GSM, SIM card and BadUSB research
card.scouting: Cracked GSM’s A5/1 encryption with rainbow tables, showed millions of SIM cards could be hijacked over the air with a text message, broke Mifare smartcards, and with Jakob Lell released BadUSB — proof that any USB device’s firmware can be reprogrammed to lie about what it is.
card.note: If it has a radio and a chip, he has probably already read the datasheet.

sources.label: A5/1, the GSM cipher his team broke

card.name: Moxie Marlinspike
card.title: Crypto for Everyone Else
card.knownFor: SSLstrip and the Signal Protocol
card.scouting: Demonstrated SSLstrip and a run of attacks that exposed how fragile the certificate authority system really was. Then built Signal and the double-ratchet protocol behind it, which WhatsApp and others adopted — quietly putting end-to-end encryption in front of billions of people.
card.note: Attacked the transport layer, then rewrote it. The set’s highest-leverage card.

card.name: Whitfield Diffie
card.title: Co-Author of Public-Key Cryptography
card.knownFor: Diffie–Hellman key exchange, and the end of the shared-secret era
card.scouting: With Martin Hellman, published “New Directions in Cryptography” in 1976 and showed that two parties who had never met could agree on a secret over a wire anyone could read. It broke a problem the field had considered permanent, and every TLS handshake since is a descendant. Shared the 2015 Turing Award for it, and spent decades afterwards arguing the civil-liberties side of the crypto policy fights.
card.note: The paper that made secure commerce on a public network conceivable at all.

card.name: Martin Hellman
card.title: Co-Author of Public-Key Cryptography
card.knownFor: Diffie–Hellman, and the fight to keep crypto research public
card.scouting: Co-author of the 1976 paper and Stanford professor who then refused to let the NSA classify academic cryptography out of existence, publishing and teaching through explicit pressure to stop. Also co-authored the early analysis of DES key length that argued, correctly and years early, that 56 bits was not enough. Shared the 2015 Turing Award with Diffie.
card.note: Won the maths, then won the argument about who is allowed to do the maths.

card.name: Ron Rivest
card.title: The R in RSA
card.knownFor: RSA, MD5, RC4 and a career of primitives everyone uses
card.scouting: Co-invented the RSA cryptosystem at MIT in 1977 with Shamir and Adleman, turning public-key cryptography from a proposal into something you could ship. Went on to design MD2, MD4, MD5, RC4, RC5 and RC6, co-author the standard algorithms textbook, and spend his later career on verifiable election systems. Turing Award, 2002.
card.note: Half the acronyms in a 1990s protocol stack trace back to one office at MIT.

card.name: Adi Shamir
card.title: The S in RSA
card.knownFor: RSA, secret sharing, and differential cryptanalysis
card.scouting: Co-invented RSA, then invented Shamir secret sharing, then co-developed differential cryptanalysis with Eli Biham — the technique that turned out to be the one the DES designers had quietly hardened against seventeen years earlier. Also a co-author of the cube attack and a long line of side-channel work. Turing Award, 2002.
card.note: Builds the lock and breaks the lock, usually in the same decade.

card.name: Leonard Adleman
card.title: The A in RSA
card.knownFor: RSA, and naming the computer virus
card.scouting: The third name on the RSA paper, whose role was to keep breaking the schemes Rivest and Shamir proposed until one survived. Later coined the term “computer virus” for Fred Cohen’s 1983 experiments, and founded DNA computing with a molecular solution to the Hamiltonian path problem. Turing Award, 2002.
card.note: The designated attacker on the RSA team. The set needs more of those.

card.name: Phil Zimmermann
card.title: Author of PGP
card.knownFor: Putting strong crypto in ordinary hands, and getting investigated for it
card.scouting: Released Pretty Good Privacy as free software in 1991, and it escaped onto the internet worldwide. The US government opened a three-year criminal investigation into him for munitions export, dropped it in 1996 without charges, and the crypto-export regime never recovered. He later co-founded Silent Circle and worked on ZRTP for encrypted voice.
card.note: The card for everyone who has ever typed a passphrase to read their own mail.

card.name: Bruce Schneier
card.title: The Field’s Public Conscience
card.knownFor: Applied Cryptography, Blowfish, and “security theatre”
card.scouting: Wrote Applied Cryptography in 1994, the book that taught a generation of engineers how ciphers actually work, then designed Blowfish and co-designed Twofish. Spent the two decades after arguing the harder point: that security is a systems and incentives problem, not a maths problem. Coined “security theatre”, has written the Crypto-Gram newsletter since 1998, and helped report on the Snowden documents.
card.note: More people entered this field because of one book than any other single cause.

card.name: Paul Kocher
card.title: The Side-Channel Pioneer
card.knownFor: Timing attacks, differential power analysis, and Spectre
card.scouting: Published the timing-attack paper in 1996 and differential power analysis in 1999, establishing that a correct implementation of a correct algorithm can still leak its key through how long it takes or how much current it draws. Co-authored the SSL 3.0 specification, founded Cryptography Research, and in 2018 was one of the co-discoverers of Spectre.
card.note: Twice made the whole industry re-audit hardware it had already shipped.

card.name: Dorothy E. Denning
card.title: Founder of Intrusion Detection
card.knownFor: The 1987 intrusion-detection model every SIEM still runs on
card.scouting: Published “An Intrusion-Detection Model” in 1987, the paper that framed detection as statistical deviation from a profile of normal behaviour and gave the entire monitoring industry its foundation. Also wrote Cryptography and Data Security, worked on database security and lattice-based information flow, and was one of the few academics engaging seriously with both sides of the Clipper chip debate.
card.note: Every alert queue in every SOC is downstream of one 1987 paper.

card.name: Gene Spafford
card.title: The Academy’s Anchor
card.knownFor: The Morris worm analysis, Practical UNIX Security, and CERIAS
card.scouting: Produced one of the first detailed technical analyses of the 1988 Morris worm while the internet was still smoking, co-wrote Practical UNIX and Internet Security with Simson Garfinkel, co-created Tripwire, and founded Purdue’s COAST lab and then CERIAS — for years the largest academic security centre in the US. Has advised more federal panels than most people have attended.
card.note: Trained a large fraction of the people on the rest of these cards.

card.name: Ross Anderson
card.title: Author of Security Engineering
card.knownFor: The textbook, and the economics of why security fails
card.scouting: Cambridge professor who wrote Security Engineering, the closest thing the field has to a canonical text, and gave away earlier editions free online. Founded the security-economics research programme with the observation that systems fail because the people who could fix them are not the people who bear the loss. Spent years demonstrating that bank chip-and-PIN systems were weaker than the banks told courts they were. Died in 2024.
card.note: If you only read one book on this list, it is this one.

card.name: Matt Blaze
card.title: The Clipper Chip Breaker
card.knownFor: Killing key escrow, then auditing the voting machines
card.scouting: Found the protocol flaw in the NSA’s Clipper chip escrow scheme in 1994 and published it, which did more to end mandated key escrow than any amount of lobbying. Later led state-commissioned source reviews of US voting systems, published work on the vulnerabilities of master-keyed physical locks and wiretap systems, and became a law-school professor arguing the same points to a different audience.
card.note: Has broken the government’s preferred backdoor design once already.

sources.label: Protocol Failure in the Escrowed Encryption Standard (1994)

card.name: Radia Perlman
card.title: Architect of Resilient Networks
card.knownFor: Spanning tree, and routing that survives a malicious node
card.scouting: Invented the spanning-tree protocol that made large bridged Ethernets possible, and did the early work on routing protocols designed to keep functioning when a participating node is actively hostile rather than merely broken. Co-wrote Network Security: Private Communication in a Public World, and designed the “ephemerizer” approach to making data reliably expire.
card.note: Designed for the assumption that some of the network is lying to you.

card.name: Steven M. Bellovin
card.title: The Protocol Sceptic
card.knownFor: Security Problems in the TCP/IP Protocol Suite, and the firewall book
card.scouting: Wrote the 1989 paper cataloguing the security problems in TCP/IP — sequence-number prediction, source routing, DNS spoofing — years before anyone was exploiting them at scale. Co-authored Firewalls and Internet Security with Cheswick, co-invented encrypted key exchange, was a Usenet co-creator, and served as chief technologist at the FTC and on the Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board.
card.note: Published the attack list first and spent thirty years watching it come true.

sources.label: Security Problems in the TCP/IP Protocol Suite (1989)

card.name: William Cheswick
card.title: The First Firewall Book
card.knownFor: Firewalls and Internet Security, and “An Evening with Berferd”
card.scouting: Co-wrote the 1994 book that taught the industry what a firewall was and how to reason about a perimeter. “An Evening with Berferd” documented him feeding a live intruder a fake environment for months and writing down everything, which is the honeypot genre’s founding text. Later ran the Internet Mapping Project at Bell Labs.
card.note: Invented the practice of watching the attacker instead of just shutting the door.

card.name: Marcus J. Ranum
card.title: Builder of the First Commercial Firewall
card.knownFor: DEC SEAL, the TIS toolkit, and thirty years of contrarianism
card.scouting: Built DEC SEAL, generally credited as the first commercial firewall product, then the TIS Firewall Toolkit and Gauntlet — the code most early internet perimeters were actually made of. Ran whitehouse.gov’s first email server. Has spent the decades since publicly arguing that most of what the industry sells does not work, which has aged better than the products did.
card.note: The perimeter, as an idea people could buy, is largely his fault and his credit.

card.name: Wietse Venema
card.title: Author of TCP Wrapper and Postfix
card.knownFor: Defensive software that a generation of admins just ran
card.scouting: Wrote TCP Wrapper, which for years was the access control on a very large share of Unix hosts on the internet, and Postfix, a mail server written from the start around privilege separation. Co-wrote SATAN with Dan Farmer and later the Coroner’s Toolkit and Forensic Discovery, giving incident responders their first real open tooling.
card.note: Shipped the defence, then shipped the tools to work out how it was beaten.

card.name: Dan Farmer
card.title: Author of COPS and SATAN
card.knownFor: Publishing the scanner, and getting fired for it
card.scouting: Wrote COPS as a student, then in 1995 released SATAN with Wietse Venema — a scanner that audited a network the way an attacker would, published openly so defenders could run it first. The press predicted the end of the internet; SGI fired him over it; the security scanner became a permanent product category. Later co-wrote Forensic Discovery.
card.note: The original argument that defenders should get the attacker’s tools too.

card.name: Gordon Lyon
card.title: Author of Nmap
card.knownFor: The scanner that is on every security laptop on earth
card.scouting: Released Nmap in Phrack in 1997 and has maintained it ever since, adding OS fingerprinting, service detection and the NSE scripting engine. Runs seclists.org, hosting the Bugtraq and Full Disclosure archives that are the field’s institutional memory, and fought MPAA and studio takedown attempts over the tool. Nmap is the first command most defenders learn.
card.note: Twenty-eight years of one maintainer. The reliability is the achievement.

card.name: Martin Roesch
card.title: Author of Snort
card.knownFor: Open-source intrusion detection, and the rule format everyone copied
card.scouting: Wrote Snort in 1998 as a lightweight packet sniffer, and it became the intrusion detection system that put IDS within reach of organisations that could never have bought one. Founded Sourcefire around it, which Cisco acquired in 2013. The Snort rule syntax outlived the product and is still how a large part of the industry writes network detections.
card.note: A weekend tool that became the de facto standard for network detection.

card.name: Gerald Combs
card.title: Author of Wireshark
card.knownFor: Making packet analysis free, and keeping it free
card.scouting: Started Ethereal in 1998 because commercial protocol analysers cost more than his employer would spend, renamed it Wireshark in 2006 after a trademark problem, and has shepherded it ever since through thousands of contributed protocol dissectors. It is the default answer to “what is actually on the wire” for network engineers and incident responders alike.
card.note: The tool you reach for when nobody can agree on what the traffic is doing.

card.name: Renaud Deraison
card.title: Author of Nessus
card.knownFor: The vulnerability scanner that defined the category
card.scouting: Released Nessus in 1998 as a free scanner with its own plugin language, at a point when the alternative was an expensive appliance. Co-founded Tenable Network Security around it in 2002 and took the product closed-source in 2005, a decision the community argued about for years. Vulnerability management as a routine operational practice largely grew out of that codebase.
card.note: The scan report that lands in an admin’s inbox every Monday started here.

card.name: Paul Vixie
card.title: Keeper of the DNS
card.knownFor: BIND, DNS RPZ, and the anti-abuse infrastructure nobody sees
card.scouting: Maintained BIND for years and wrote or co-wrote a long run of DNS RFCs, then built the response-policy zone mechanism that lets defenders block malicious domains at the resolver. Founded the first anti-spam DNSBL, ran the Internet Software Consortium, operates F-root, and co-founded Farsight Security around passive DNS. Internet Hall of Fame, 2014.
card.note: Ran the plumbing, then built the filters when the plumbing got abused.

card.name: Niels Provos
card.title: Honeypots and Safe Browsing
card.knownFor: honeyd, bcrypt, and warning a billion browsers
card.scouting: Wrote honeyd, co-designed the bcrypt password hash with David Mazières, and created systrace and privilege separation work in OpenSSH. At Google he led the Safe Browsing malware research that put interstitial warnings in front of drive-by download sites, and co-authored the papers that measured how large that problem actually was.
card.note: bcrypt alone has protected more passwords than most companies have users.

card.name: Jeremiah Grossman
card.title: The Web Application Security Authority
card.knownFor: XSS Attacks, WhiteHat Security, and making web appsec a discipline
card.scouting: Was an information security officer at Yahoo before founding WhiteHat Security in 2001, where continuous scanning of thousands of production sites produced the first credible public statistics on how long real web vulnerabilities actually stay open. Co-founded the Web Application Security Consortium, and co-authored XSS Attacks: Cross Site Scripting Exploits and Defense in 2007 — the book that turned cross-site scripting from a curiosity into a class of bug developers were expected to know.
card.note: The XSS book is still the reference. Web appsec became a discipline on his watch.

sources.label: XSS Attacks: Cross Site Scripting Exploits and Defense

card.name: Robert Hansen
card.title: The XSS Cheat Sheet
card.knownFor: ha.ckers.org, Slowloris, and browser attack surface
card.scouting: Ran ha.ckers.org and published the XSS cheat sheet, which for years was the reference list of filter-evasion payloads that every web application firewall was tested against. Co-authored XSS Attacks with Grossman, released Slowloris to demonstrate that a single machine could hold a web server’s connections open indefinitely, and co-wrote Detecting Malice on behavioural detection.
card.note: The cheat sheet did more for input validation than any standards document.

sources.label: XSS Attacks: Cross Site Scripting Exploits and Defense

card.name: Mark Curphey
card.title: Founder of OWASP
card.knownFor: Starting the open project that appsec organised itself around
card.scouting: Started the Open Web Application Security Project in September 2001 as a mailing list and a few documents, and it became the vendor-neutral body that produced the Top Ten, the ASVS, ZAP and the testing guides that appsec teams still work from. Later founded SourceClear on software composition analysis and has kept publicly pushing OWASP to stay relevant to modern supply-chain risk.
card.note: Built the commons the whole application security industry now cites.

card.name: Jeff Williams
card.title: Author of the First OWASP Top Ten
card.knownFor: The list every compliance regime ended up pointing at
card.scouting: Wrote the first OWASP Top Ten and served as the volunteer chair of OWASP from 2003 to 2011, the years in which it went from a mailing list to the reference that PCI DSS and a long line of other standards cite by name. Co-founded Aspect Security and then Contrast Security, arguing for instrumentation inside the running application rather than scanning it from outside.
card.note: One list, and suddenly every auditor knew what SQL injection was.

card.name: Gary McGraw
card.title: Building Security In
card.knownFor: Software security as a discipline, and BSIMM
card.scouting: Wrote Building Secure Software, Exploiting Software and Software Security, making the case that you cannot test defects out of a system you designed insecurely. Co-created BSIMM, which measures what security programmes actually do rather than what a standard says they should, and has run a long-standing interview series documenting the field’s own history.
card.note: Moved the argument from “scan it later” to “design it right”.

card.name: Michael Howard
card.title: Author of Writing Secure Code
card.knownFor: The book and the process behind Microsoft’s security turnaround
card.scouting: Co-wrote Writing Secure Code, which Bill Gates ordered Windows engineers to read during the 2002 Trustworthy Computing halt, and helped build the Security Development Lifecycle that came out of it — threat modelling, banned APIs, fuzzing and a final security review before ship. The SDL became the template most large software organisations copied.
card.note: Turned “be careful” into a checklist an entire company could be held to.

card.name: Adam Shostack
card.title: The Threat Modelling Canon
card.knownFor: Threat Modeling: Designing for Security, and STRIDE in practice
card.scouting: Drove threat modelling into shippable practice at Microsoft, including the Elevation of Privilege card game that got non-security engineers doing it voluntarily, then wrote Threat Modeling: Designing for Security and later Threats: What Every Engineer Should Learn. Served on the CVE editorial board and co-wrote The New School of Information Security on learning from breach data.
card.note: Four questions — what are we building, what can go wrong, what do we do, did we do a good job.

sources.label: Elevation of Privilege threat modelling game

card.name: Ivan Ristić
card.title: Author of ModSecurity and SSL Labs
card.knownFor: Grading the internet’s TLS, one hostname at a time
card.scouting: Wrote ModSecurity, the open-source web application firewall that became the reference implementation and the base of the OWASP Core Rule Set. Then built SSL Labs, whose A-to-F grade for a server’s TLS configuration turned an obscure ops detail into something executives asked about, and wrote Bulletproof TLS and PKI as the manual for fixing the grade.
card.note: Made bad TLS visible and embarrassing, which fixed more of it than any RFC.

card.name: Mark Dowd
card.title: The Art of Software Security Assessment
card.knownFor: The code-audit bible, and the Sendmail and Flash bugs behind it
card.scouting: Co-wrote The Art of Software Security Assessment with John McDonald and Justin Schuh, still the most thorough published treatment of how to find memory-safety and logic flaws by reading code. Found deep bugs in Sendmail, OpenSSH and Flash while at ISS X-Force and IBM, and founded Azimuth Security. His work is why a generation of auditors know what to look for in a parser.
card.note: The book that turned code review from a chore into a craft.

sources.label: The Art of Software Security Assessment

card.name: Thomas Dullien
card.title: The Binary Diffing Pioneer
card.knownFor: BinDiff, and the theory of weird machines
card.scouting: Built the graph-based binary diffing that made it routine to extract the vulnerability out of a vendor patch, founded zynamics around BinDiff and VxClass, and sold it to Google in 2011. Later worked in Project Zero and wrote the “weird machines” framing that treats exploitation as programming an unintended state machine inside the target.
card.note: Turned Patch Tuesday into a reliable source of exploit intelligence.

card.name: Alex Sotirov
card.title: The Rogue CA Demonstration
card.knownFor: MD5 collisions against a real certificate authority
card.scouting: Co-authored “Bypassing Browser Memory Protections”, the 2008 paper that showed how attackers were routing around DEP and ASLR, then at 25C3 the same year demonstrated a working rogue certificate authority built on MD5 collisions — which pushed the CA industry off MD5 for good. Co-founded Trail of Bits.
card.note: Demonstrated the theoretical break against a live CA, which is the only kind that moves anyone.

card.name: Thomas Ptacek
card.title: The IDS Evasion Paper
card.knownFor: Insertion, Evasion and Denial of Service, and Matasano
card.scouting: Co-wrote the 1998 paper with Timothy Newsham showing that a network IDS which reassembles traffic differently from the host it protects can be walked straight past — the work that forced every vendor to rethink normalisation. Co-founded Matasano and later Latacora, and wrote the Cryptopals challenges that taught a generation how crypto actually breaks.
card.note: One paper made every IDS vendor rewrite their TCP stack.

sources.label: Insertion, Evasion, and Denial of Service (1998)

card.name: Matthew D. Green
card.title: The Cryptography Auditor
card.knownFor: TrueCrypt audit, and explaining broken crypto in public
card.scouting: Johns Hopkins cryptographer who co-led the Open Crypto Audit Project’s review of TrueCrypt, contributed to the analysis of Dual_EC_DRBG and the RSA BSAFE backdoor, and worked on the attacks behind Logjam and DROWN. His blog is the standard place the rest of the industry goes to find out how badly a new crypto story is being reported.
card.note: Does the audit, then does the translation so the rest of us can follow it.

sources.label: A Few Thoughts on Cryptographic Engineering

card.name: J. Alex Halderman
card.title: The Voting Machine Auditor
card.knownFor: Cold boot attacks, election security, and Let’s Encrypt
card.scouting: Co-authored the cold boot attack paper showing DRAM retains keys after power off, then spent a career demonstrating — in court and in front of legislatures — that deployed voting machines could be reprogrammed. Co-founded the Internet Security Research Group behind Let’s Encrypt, and co-authored the ZMap internet-wide scanner and the Logjam and FREAK results.
card.note: Let’s Encrypt alone changed the default state of the web from plaintext to TLS.

sources.label: Lest We Remember: Cold Boot Attacks on Encryption Keys

card.name: Nadia Heninger
card.title: The Key-Entropy Auditor
card.knownFor: Mining Your Ps and Qs, Logjam, and measuring real deployed crypto
card.scouting: Co-authored “Mining Your Ps and Qs”, which scanned the whole IPv4 internet and found that a meaningful share of TLS and SSH keys shared factors because embedded devices generated them without entropy — and then factored them. Followed it with Logjam, DROWN and FREAK, a body of work whose method is: measure what is actually deployed, then break the weak part.
card.note: Proved the crypto was fine and the random number generators were not.

sources.label: Mining Your Ps and Qs (USENIX Security 2012)

card.name: Troy Hunt
card.title: Keeper of Have I Been Pwned
card.knownFor: Turning breach data into a public service
card.scouting: Built Have I Been Pwned in 2013 as a way for ordinary people to find out whether their account was in a dump, and it became infrastructure: browsers, password managers and the NIST-endorsed practice of checking passwords against known-breached lists all query it, using a k-anonymity scheme that never sends the password. Runs it as a public good rather than a product.
card.note: One person’s side project ended up inside the login flow of half the web.

card.name: Window Snyder
card.title: The Serial Security Chief
card.knownFor: Windows XP SP2, Firefox, Apple, Intel, and Threat Modeling
card.scouting: Was security lead and signoff for Windows XP Service Pack 2 and Windows Server 2003, co-wrote the Threat Modeling book that came out of that era, then ran security at Mozilla for Firefox, at Apple on privacy and security strategy, at Fastly and Square, and became Intel’s first chief software security officer. Founded Thistle Technologies in 2020 to bring update infrastructure to embedded devices.
card.note: Has been the person accountable for a shipping product’s security more times than anyone.

card.name: Heather Adkins
card.title: Google’s Founding Defender
card.knownFor: Twenty-plus years of Google security, and Operation Aurora
card.scouting: A founding member of Google’s security team who built and ran its incident response function, including the response to the 2009 Operation Aurora intrusion that Google chose to disclose publicly — a decision that reset industry norms on breach transparency. Co-authored Building Secure and Reliable Systems, and has served on US federal cybersecurity advisory bodies.
card.note: Ran the response that made public disclosure of a state intrusion normal.

card.name: Parisa Tabriz
card.title: Google’s Security Princess
card.knownFor: Chrome security, and the campaign that made HTTPS the default
card.scouting: Joined Google as a penetration tester, printed “Security Princess” on her business card, and rose to run Chrome. Led the multi-year project to mark plain HTTP as “Not secure” in the world’s most-used browser, which more than anything else moved the web to encryption by default, and pushed Project Zero’s 90-day disclosure deadline as an industry-wide forcing function.
card.note: Changed one string in a browser UI and moved the whole web to TLS.

sources.label: Chromium: marking HTTP as not secure

card.name: Alex Stamos
card.title: The CSO Who Resigned Over It
card.knownFor: Yahoo, Facebook, and saying the uncomfortable thing in public
card.scouting: Was CISO at Yahoo, where he objected to a government email-scanning programme, then CSO at Facebook through the investigation into foreign influence operations, leaving in 2018 over how much the company would disclose. Publicly challenged the NSA director on encryption backdoors, founded the Stanford Internet Observatory, and co-founded iSEC Partners and later Krebs Stamos Group.
card.note: The card about what the job costs when you do it honestly.

card.name: Dan Geer
card.title: The Field’s Dissenting Economist
card.knownFor: CyberInsecurity: The Cost of Monopoly, and getting fired for it
card.scouting: Co-authored the 2003 CCIA report arguing that monoculture in operating systems was itself a national security risk, and was fired by @stake, then a Microsoft consultancy, the day it was published. Went on to serve as chief information security officer of In-Q-Tel and to give a run of Black Hat and USENIX keynotes that are still the most quoted long-form arguments about security policy the field has produced.
card.note: Paid for the paper with his job, and the paper was right.

card.name: Kevin Mandia
card.title: The Incident Response Industry
card.knownFor: Mandiant, and the APT1 report that named the unit
card.scouting: Founded Mandiant in 2004 and built breach response into a business that governments and Fortune 100 boards call at 2am. In 2013 the company published APT1, a report attributing years of intrusions to a specific People’s Liberation Army unit with building photographs and operator handles — the moment public, named attribution became something private companies did.
card.note: Made attribution a commercial deliverable instead of a classified one.

sources.label: APT1: Exposing One of China’s Cyber Espionage Units (2013)

card.name: Mikko Hyppönen
card.title: The Malware Historian
card.knownFor: Three decades at F-Secure, and finding the authors of Brain
card.scouting: Has been analysing malware at F-Secure since 1991, through the DOS virus era, Sasser and Blaster, Stuxnet and modern ransomware. Tracked down and interviewed the Pakistani brothers who wrote Brain, the first PC virus, twenty years after the fact. Formulated Hyppönen’s law — if it is smart, it is vulnerable — and is the researcher most often trusted to explain a live incident to the public.
card.note: The continuity card. One person watched the entire history of malware happen.

card.name: Robert M. Lee
card.title: The Industrial Control Defender
card.knownFor: Dragos, and the analysis of the Ukraine grid attacks
card.scouting: A former US Air Force cyber warfare officer who co-authored the analysis of the 2015 Ukrainian power grid attack and the later CRASHOVERRIDE and TRISIS malware, then founded Dragos to do industrial control system defence as a specialism rather than an IT afterthought. Co-wrote the SANS ICS courses that most OT defenders come through.
card.note: The set’s reminder that some networks fail into a physical consequence.

sources.label: Analysis of the Cyber Attack on the Ukrainian Power Grid (SANS/E-ISAC, 2016)

card.name: Lesley Carhart
card.title: The Industrial Incident Responder
card.knownFor: OT forensics, and teaching the field how to get into the field
card.scouting: Led incident response at Motorola Solutions and then at Dragos, running investigations inside live industrial networks where you cannot simply reimage the plant. Writes long-running public guidance on breaking into and surviving the profession, founded PancakesCon, and holds the SANS Lifetime Achievement Award for that work as much as the casework.
card.note: The mentorship is the contribution. Half a conference floor learned from those posts.

card.name: Katie Nickels
card.title: The ATT&CK Translator
card.knownFor: MITRE ATT&CK threat intelligence, and making CTI actionable
card.scouting: Was the threat intelligence lead for MITRE ATT&CK during the years it became the shared vocabulary defenders use to describe adversary behaviour, then went to Red Canary as director of intelligence. Teaches the SANS cyber threat intelligence course and spends most of her public work on the unglamorous question of how an intelligence report turns into a detection someone actually deploys.
card.note: ATT&CK gave the blue team a language. This is the card for the person who taught it.

card.name: Geoffrey Hinton
card.title: The Godfather of Deep Learning
card.knownFor: Backpropagation, and thirty years of being right too early
card.scouting: Co-authored the 1986 paper that made backpropagation practical, then spent the AI winter insisting neural networks would work while the field moved on. Was proved right in 2012 when his students won ImageNet by a margin nobody could argue with. Shared the 2018 Turing Award and the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics, and left Google to speak freely about the risks.
card.note: The whole field is downstream of one person refusing to change his mind.

card.name: Yann LeCun
card.title: Architect of the Convolutional Net
card.knownFor: LeNet, and pushing Meta to release its models
card.scouting: Built LeNet in the late 1980s and had convolutional networks reading cheques at industrial scale while the rest of the field doubted them. Shared the 2018 Turing Award. As Meta’s chief AI scientist he has been the loudest senior voice for releasing weights rather than gatekeeping them, which is a large part of why open-weight models exist at all.
card.note: The open-weight ecosystem has one very stubborn advocate to thank.

sources.label: Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition (1998)

card.name: Yoshua Bengio
card.title: The Academic Conscience
card.knownFor: Deep learning theory, Theano, and the turn to safety
card.scouting: Third of the 2018 Turing Award trio, and the one who stayed in the university. Founded MILA, whose lab produced Theano — the framework a generation of researchers learned on before TensorFlow and PyTorch existed. Co-authored the Deep Learning textbook, and now chairs international scientific reporting on AI risk.
card.note: Kept the research public when the money was arguing for the opposite.

card.name: Jürgen Schmidhuber
card.title: Author of the LSTM
card.knownFor: Long short-term memory, and insisting he did it first
card.scouting: With Sepp Hochreiter published long short-term memory in 1997, the architecture that made sequence learning work and which ran speech recognition and translation on a billion phones before transformers arrived. Also did early work on meta-learning, artificial curiosity and GAN-adjacent ideas, and is famous for pointing out, at length, when the field forgets its own history.
card.note: Difficult, frequently correct, and the priority disputes are usually worth reading.

card.name: Richard S. Sutton
card.title: The Bitter Lesson
card.knownFor: Reinforcement learning, and the essay that keeps being right
card.scouting: Invented temporal-difference learning and co-wrote Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction, the textbook the whole field learned from and which is free online. His 2019 essay “The Bitter Lesson” — that general methods plus compute beat handcrafted human knowledge — has become the most-cited two pages in modern AI. Shared the 2024 Turing Award.
card.note: Wrote the shortest, most annoying, most consistently vindicated thing in AI.

card.name: Andrew Barto
card.title: Co-Founder of Reinforcement Learning
card.knownFor: Actor-critic methods and the RL textbook
card.scouting: With Sutton, built reinforcement learning into a coherent field from the actor-critic architecture onward, and co-wrote the textbook that defined it. His work tied machine learning back to animal learning and dopamine-driven reward prediction, which turned out to describe both. Shared the 2024 Turing Award.
card.note: The quieter half of the pair that gave machines a reason to try things.

card.name: Judea Pearl
card.title: The Causality Argument
card.knownFor: Bayesian networks, do-calculus, and what deep learning cannot do
card.scouting: Made probabilistic reasoning tractable with Bayesian networks, then built the formal machinery of causal inference — do-calculus, counterfactuals, the ladder of causation. Turing Award, 2011. Spends much of his time arguing that systems which only fit correlations are missing the thing that makes reasoning work, an argument the scaling era has not settled.
card.note: The standing objection the field has not answered, only outrun.

card.name: Fei-Fei Li
card.title: Creator of ImageNet
card.knownFor: The dataset that started the deep learning era
card.scouting: Built ImageNet when the field believed better algorithms mattered more than more data, and gave it away. The 2012 competition on that dataset is the moment deep learning stopped being a minority position. Founded Stanford HAI, served as chief scientist of AI at Google Cloud, and has pushed hard on who gets a say in how this technology is built.
card.note: Proved the data was the bottleneck, then handed the data to everyone.

card.name: Ashish Vaswani
card.title: First Author on the Transformer
card.knownFor: Attention Is All You Need
card.scouting: Lead author of the 2017 paper that threw out recurrence and convolution and kept only attention. Every large language model since is a transformer, which makes those eight pages the most consequential architecture paper of the century so far. Later co-founded Adept and then Essential AI.
card.note: One paper, and the shape of every model you have used since.

card.name: Noam Shazeer
card.title: The Efficiency Obsessive
card.knownFor: The Transformer, mixture-of-experts, and Character.AI
card.scouting: Transformer co-author whose fingerprints are on most of what made the architecture fast: multi-query attention, sparsely-gated mixture-of-experts, the Mesh-TensorFlow work on model parallelism, and the T5 line. Left Google to found Character.AI, then returned to lead Gemini. Widely regarded as the best engineer in the room on making big models cheap.
card.note: Designed it, then spent a decade making it affordable to run.

sources.label: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts (2017)

card.name: Łukasz Kaiser
card.title: The One Who Open-Sourced It
card.knownFor: The Transformer, Tensor2Tensor and Trax
card.scouting: Transformer co-author who also built and released Tensor2Tensor, the open library that put a working transformer implementation in everyone’s hands within weeks of the paper, and later Trax. Moved to OpenAI to work on the reasoning-model line. The gap between publishing an architecture and everyone being able to run it was largely his to close.
card.note: The paper made it famous; the repo made it everyone’s.

card.name: Aidan Gomez
card.title: The Youngest Author
card.knownFor: The Transformer, and building Cohere
card.scouting: Was an intern when he became a co-author on Attention Is All You Need. Co-founded FOR.ai and then Cohere, building large language models for enterprises, and Cohere Labs has released open-weight multilingual models including the Aya family with a strong emphasis on languages the field usually ignores.
card.note: Went from intern on the paper to running a lab built on it.

card.name: Alex Krizhevsky
card.title: Author of AlexNet
card.knownFor: The 2012 result that ended the argument
card.scouting: Wrote the CUDA code that trained AlexNet on two consumer GPUs and won ImageNet 2012 by a margin so large it settled the question of whether deep learning worked. Released cuda-convnet so others could reproduce it. Also assembled CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, which remain the default first datasets for anyone learning the field.
card.note: Hand-wrote the kernels that started the modern era, then went quiet.

card.name: Ilya Sutskever
card.title: The Scaling Believer
card.knownFor: AlexNet, seq2seq, and the GPT line
card.scouting: Co-author of AlexNet, then of sequence-to-sequence learning, then co-founder and chief scientist of OpenAI through the GPT series. The through-line of his career is a conviction that scale plus the right objective gets you most of the way, held earlier and harder than almost anyone. Left in 2024 to found Safe Superintelligence.
card.note: Bet on scale before it was obvious, three separate times.

sources.label: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks (2014)

card.name: Ian Goodfellow
card.title: Inventor of the GAN
card.knownFor: Generative adversarial networks
card.scouting: Proposed generative adversarial networks in 2014 — two networks trained against each other — and gave image generation its first decade. Co-wrote the Deep Learning textbook with Bengio and Courville, which is free to read online, and did foundational work on adversarial examples that became its own subfield.
card.note: Two networks arguing, and suddenly machines could imagine.

card.name: Tri Dao
card.title: Author of FlashAttention
card.knownFor: Making attention fit in memory, and co-creating Mamba
card.scouting: Wrote FlashAttention, an IO-aware exact attention kernel that cut memory use enough to make long contexts practical, and released it openly — it is now in essentially every training stack in the world. Co-created the Mamba state space architecture with Albert Gu, also open. Chief scientist at Together AI and a Princeton professor.
card.note: If your context window is long, it is partly because of his CUDA.

card.name: Albert Gu
card.title: The State Space Alternative
card.knownFor: S4 and Mamba, the credible challenge to attention
card.scouting: Developed structured state space models — S4 and its successors — showing that sequence modelling with linear-time scaling could compete with quadratic attention on long inputs. Co-created Mamba with Tri Dao and released it openly. The most serious architectural alternative to the transformer to come out of the last decade.
card.note: The only person with a real answer to "what comes after attention".

sources.label: Efficiently Modeling Long Sequences with Structured State Spaces (2021)

card.name: Alec Radford
card.title: The Quiet Architect of GPT
card.knownFor: GPT, CLIP and Whisper
card.scouting: First author on the original GPT paper, on GPT-2, on CLIP and on Whisper — an unusual concentration of foundational work in one person. DCGAN before that. Whisper was released openly with weights and remains the default speech recognition model for anyone who does not want to send audio to an API.
card.note: Four papers, four subfields. Almost no public profile.

sources.label: Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training (2018)

card.name: David Silver
card.title: Architect of AlphaGo
card.knownFor: AlphaGo, AlphaZero and learning without human data
card.scouting: Led the AlphaGo work that beat Lee Sedol in 2016, a result the field had expected to be a decade away, then AlphaZero — which threw away the human games entirely and taught itself Go, chess and shogi from the rules. His RL lecture series, free on YouTube, taught the subject to a generation.
card.note: Showed that removing the human data made it stronger, not weaker.

sources.label: Mastering the game of Go without human knowledge (2017)

card.name: Oriol Vinyals
card.title: From Seq2Seq to Gemini
card.knownFor: Sequence-to-sequence, AlphaStar, and leading Gemini
card.scouting: Co-authored sequence-to-sequence learning and Pointer Networks, led AlphaStar to grandmaster level at StarCraft II — a far messier problem than board games — and is now a lead on Gemini. One of the few researchers whose career spans the pre-transformer, game-playing and frontier-model eras at the top of each.
card.note: Has been at the front of three different eras of the field.

card.name: John Jumper
card.title: Architect of AlphaFold
card.knownFor: Solving protein structure prediction, and releasing it
card.scouting: Led AlphaFold 2, which solved a fifty-year-old grand challenge in biology to experimental accuracy. DeepMind then released the code and predicted structures for essentially every known protein, free, which is the part biologists actually talk about. Shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
card.note: The strongest argument in the set that AI can just make a field better.

sources.label: Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold (2021)

card.name: Shane Legg
card.title: The One Who Said AGI
card.knownFor: Co-founding DeepMind and defining machine intelligence
card.scouting: Co-founded DeepMind with Hassabis and Suleyman and is chief AGI scientist there. His doctoral work with Marcus Hutter produced a formal definition of machine intelligence, and he popularised the term AGI at a point when saying it out loud was a career risk. Has publicly held a rough timeline for human-level AI since 2011.
card.note: Was using the word AGI in public when it still got you laughed at.

sources.label: Universal Intelligence: A Definition of Machine Intelligence (2007)

card.name: Demis Hassabis
card.title: Founder of DeepMind
card.knownFor: AlphaGo, AlphaFold, and a Nobel Prize
card.scouting: Chess prodigy, then games developer, then neuroscientist, then founder of DeepMind — the lab that produced DQN, AlphaGo, AlphaZero and AlphaFold. Shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the last of those. Has been consistent for two decades that the point of building intelligence is to use it on science.
card.note: The rare lab founder who kept doing the research himself.

card.name: Pieter Abbeel
card.title: Robots That Learn
card.knownFor: Deep reinforcement learning for real machines
card.scouting: Berkeley professor who moved deep RL out of simulators and onto physical robots, with apprenticeship learning, domain randomisation and the BAIR lab’s long run of open releases. Co-founded Covariant, and his Deep RL Bootcamp and course materials are freely available and are how a lot of people learned the subject.
