card.note: The bridge between a policy that works in sim and an arm that works.

card.name: Andrej Karpathy
card.title: The Great Explainer
card.knownFor: nanoGPT, micrograd, llm.c, and teaching the whole internet
card.scouting: Founding member of OpenAI, then director of AI at Tesla, but the reason he is on this card is the teaching: char-rnn, CS231n, micrograd, nanoGPT, llm.c and the Zero to Hero series, all free, all readable. He has probably taught more working engineers how a transformer actually works than every university course combined.
card.note: The openness score is not a typo. Nobody else in this set is close.

card.name: Jeff Dean
card.title: The Infrastructure
card.knownFor: MapReduce, TensorFlow, TPUs and Google Brain
card.scouting: Built much of the distributed systems layer modern computing runs on — MapReduce, BigTable, Spanner — then co-founded Google Brain and drove DistBelief, TensorFlow and the TPU programme. TensorFlow being released openly in 2015 is a large part of why the deep learning boom was not confined to a handful of labs.
card.note: Open-sourcing TensorFlow did more for the field than most research.

card.name: Rajat Monga
card.title: The TensorFlow Lead
card.knownFor: Turning DistBelief into something the public could use
card.scouting: Led TensorFlow engineering at Google, taking the internal DistBelief system and shipping it as an open-source framework with a public API, documentation and a community. For several years TensorFlow was simply how machine learning was done outside a handful of labs, and that was an engineering and release-management achievement as much as a research one.
card.note: Somebody has to make the internal thing safe to hand to strangers.

sources.label: TensorFlow: A system for large-scale machine learning (2016)

card.name: Soumith Chintala
card.title: The Face of PyTorch
card.knownFor: The framework the research world actually switched to
card.scouting: Co-created and led PyTorch, which won the research community by being straightforwardly pleasant to debug when the alternative was not. Ran it as a genuinely open project with an unusually visible maintainer, shepherded it into the Linux Foundation, and co-authored DCGAN along the way. Almost every model in this set was trained in his framework.
card.note: Won by making the thing nice to use, which nobody else tried.

sources.label: PyTorch: An Imperative Style, High-Performance Deep Learning Library (2019)

card.name: Adam Paszke
card.title: PyTorch and JAX
card.knownFor: Writing the autograd everyone uses
card.scouting: Wrote the original PyTorch autograd engine as a student and is first author on the PyTorch paper, then moved to Google and became a core author of JAX. Two of the three frameworks serious research runs on have his design decisions inside them, which is an unusual thing to be able to say.
card.note: The differentiation engine under two ecosystems at once.

sources.label: PyTorch: An Imperative Style, High-Performance Deep Learning Library (2019)

card.name: Tianqi Chen
card.title: The Serial Framework Author
card.knownFor: XGBoost, MXNet, TVM and MLC
card.scouting: Wrote XGBoost, which won a remarkable share of Kaggle competitions and is still the default for tabular data. Then co-created MXNet, then Apache TVM for compiling models to any hardware, then MLC-LLM for running models on phones and browsers. Every one of them open, and each solved a bottleneck the field was about to hit.
card.note: Four separate pieces of infrastructure, all still in use, all given away.

card.name: Yangqing Jia
card.title: Author of Caffe
card.knownFor: The first framework deep learning had
card.scouting: Wrote Caffe as a Berkeley PhD student and released it, giving computer vision its first widely usable deep learning framework at exactly the moment the field needed one. Later built Caffe2 at Facebook, co-created ONNX so models could move between frameworks, and led large-scale AI infrastructure at Alibaba before founding Lepton AI.
card.note: Before PyTorch and TensorFlow there was one option, and he wrote it.

sources.label: Caffe: Convolutional Architecture for Fast Feature Embedding (2014)

card.name: François Chollet
card.title: Author of Keras
card.knownFor: The API that made neural networks approachable, and ARC
card.scouting: Wrote Keras, whose entire premise was that building a neural network should not require a PhD in the framework, and it became the on-ramp for an enormous number of practitioners. Also created the ARC benchmark and its prize, a deliberate test of fluid reasoning that current models still find hard — a useful corrective to benchmark saturation.
card.note: Made it easy, then built the benchmark arguing easy is not the same as smart.

sources.label: On the Measure of Intelligence / ARC (2019)

card.name: Thomas Wolf
card.title: The Transformers Library
card.knownFor: Making every published model a one-line import
card.scouting: Co-founder and chief scientist of Hugging Face, and the driving force behind the transformers library, which turned "reproduce this paper" from a week of work into an import statement. Led the BigScience collaboration that produced BLOOM, one of the first genuinely open large multilingual models, built by a thousand researchers in the open.
card.note: Compressed the distance between a paper and a working model to nothing.

card.name: Clément Delangue
card.title: The Hub
card.knownFor: Building the place open models live
card.scouting: Co-founded Hugging Face and turned it from a chatbot app into the default distribution point for open models, datasets and demos. Whatever you think of the company, the Hub is the reason an open-weight release can reach everyone the day it lands, and the reason a small lab can ship a model at all.
card.note: Not a researcher. Built the infrastructure open research needed to matter.

card.name: Georgi Gerganov
card.title: Author of llama.cpp
card.knownFor: Putting large models on ordinary hardware
card.scouting: Wrote ggml, whisper.cpp and llama.cpp — dependency-free C implementations that run large models on laptops, phones and Raspberry Pis. The GGUF format and its quantisation schemes are how most people actually run a model locally. Arguably did more for practical access to open models than any lab release.
card.note: One person, plain C, and suddenly the models ran on your own machine.

card.name: Tim Dettmers
card.title: The Quantisation Guy
card.knownFor: bitsandbytes and QLoRA
card.scouting: Worked out how to run and fine-tune large models in 8-bit and then 4-bit without wrecking them, shipped it as bitsandbytes, and followed with QLoRA — which put fine-tuning a 65B model on a single consumer GPU. His hardware guides are the reference for anyone deciding what to buy.
card.note: Turned "you need a datacentre" into "you need one good GPU".

sources.label: QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs (2023)

card.name: Jeremy Howard
card.title: Teacher and Agitator
card.knownFor: fast.ai, ULMFiT, and arguing for open models in public
card.scouting: Co-authored ULMFiT, which brought transfer learning to NLP before the GPT line, and founded fast.ai, whose free courses and library have trained an enormous number of practitioners on the premise that you do not need a PhD to do this. Has been one of the most persistent public voices against regulating open-weight models out of existence.
card.note: Teaches for free and then goes and argues with legislators about it.

card.name: Stella Biderman
card.title: Open Models, Open Data
card.knownFor: EleutherAI, GPT-NeoX and Pythia
card.scouting: Executive director of EleutherAI, the volunteer collective that trained and released GPT-Neo, GPT-J and GPT-NeoX when nothing comparable was public, and built the Pile. Led Pythia, a suite of models released with every training checkpoint and the data order — which made a whole class of interpretability and memorisation research possible for the first time.
card.note: Released the checkpoints, not just the model. That is the contribution.

sources.label: Pythia: A Suite for Analyzing Large Language Models (2023)

card.name: Justine Tunney
card.title: One File, Runs Anywhere
card.knownFor: llamafile and Cosmopolitan Libc
card.scouting: Wrote Cosmopolitan Libc, which produces a single binary that runs natively on Linux, macOS, Windows and BSD, then used it to build llamafile — a whole language model and its runtime in one executable file you can copy to a machine and run. Also contributed substantial CPU inference speedups back to llama.cpp.
card.note: Distribution as an engineering problem, solved with unreasonable rigour.

card.name: Guillaume Lample
card.title: Lead Author of LLaMA
card.knownFor: The model release that created the open-weight ecosystem
card.scouting: Led LLaMA at Meta, showing that a smaller model trained on far more tokens beat much larger ones — and then it reached the public. Nearly every open fine-tune, quantisation and local-inference project of the following two years traces to those weights. Co-founded Mistral, which has kept releasing open-weight models under permissive licences.
card.note: The weights that turned open-source AI from an argument into an ecosystem.

sources.label: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models (2023)

card.name: Arthur Mensch
card.title: Europe’s Open Lab
card.knownFor: Mistral, and shipping open weights as a business
card.scouting: Worked on Chinchilla and Flamingo at DeepMind, then co-founded Mistral and released Mistral 7B and Mixtral under Apache 2.0 — models good enough that "open weights" stopped being a compromise. Made the case, commercially rather than rhetorically, that a frontier lab can give the weights away and still have a business.
card.note: Proved open weights and a real company are not mutually exclusive.

card.name: Robin Rombach
card.title: Author of Latent Diffusion
card.knownFor: Stable Diffusion
card.scouting: Lead author of the latent diffusion paper — run the diffusion in a compressed latent space and image generation suddenly fits on a consumer GPU — which became Stable Diffusion. Its open release in 2022 put image generation in everyone’s hands overnight and set off both an explosion of tooling and a still-unresolved argument about training data.
card.note: The single release that made generative imagery a public technology.

sources.label: High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models (2021)

card.name: Patrick Esser
card.title: The Other Half of Diffusion
card.knownFor: VQGAN, latent diffusion and Stable Diffusion 3
card.scouting: Co-authored VQGAN — the taming-transformers work that made high-resolution generation tractable — and then latent diffusion and Stable Diffusion. Later led the rectified-flow architecture behind Stable Diffusion 3 and moved to Black Forest Labs for the FLUX models, which were also released with open weights.
card.note: Two labs, three architectures, and the weights kept coming out.

sources.label: Taming Transformers for High-Resolution Image Synthesis (2020)

card.name: Christoph Schuhmann
card.title: Founder of LAION
card.knownFor: The open datasets the image models were trained on
card.scouting: A schoolteacher who organised a volunteer effort to assemble LAION-400M and LAION-5B, the open image-text datasets that Stable Diffusion and OpenCLIP were trained on. Before LAION, the data behind multimodal models was private by default; afterwards, anyone could inspect it — including the researchers who found serious problems in it.
card.note: Made the training data auditable, which is how its flaws got found.

card.name: Joelle Pineau
card.title: The Reproducibility Enforcer
card.knownFor: Running Meta AI research, and the reproducibility checklist
card.scouting: McGill professor and long-time head of Meta’s AI research, during which FAIR released PyTorch, LLaMA, and a long run of open models and code. Created the machine learning reproducibility checklist adopted by NeurIPS, forcing the field to state its assumptions and publish enough to be checked.
card.note: Made "show your work" a condition of publication at the biggest venue.

card.name: Chris Olah
card.title: Opening the Black Box
card.knownFor: Distill, feature visualisation and mechanistic interpretability
card.scouting: Did the feature-visualisation and circuits work that turned "what is the network doing" from a shrug into a research programme, and co-founded Distill to publish it in a form people could actually understand. Co-founded Anthropic, where the interpretability team continues to publish its findings openly.
card.note: Made the insides of a model legible, and made the explanations beautiful.

sources.label: Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits (2020)

card.name: Paul Christiano
card.title: The RLHF Paper
card.knownFor: Learning from human preferences
card.scouting: Lead author of deep reinforcement learning from human preferences, the technique that became RLHF and turned raw language models into things that follow instructions — the single largest reason chat assistants work at all. Later founded the Alignment Research Center and moved to the US AI Safety Institute.
card.note: Wrote the alignment paper that turned out to also be the product paper.

sources.label: Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences (2017)

card.name: Jan Leike
card.title: The Alignment Lead
card.knownFor: InstructGPT, superalignment, and resigning over it
card.scouting: Co-led the work that turned RLHF into InstructGPT and then ChatGPT, and headed OpenAI’s superalignment effort. Resigned publicly in 2024 saying safety culture had lost out to shipping, which is a rare thing for someone at that level to say on the record, and moved to Anthropic to continue the work.
card.note: Built the alignment method, then said out loud when it was being sidelined.

sources.label: Training language models to follow instructions (2022)

card.name: Stuart Russell
card.title: The Textbook and the Warning
card.knownFor: Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach
card.scouting: Co-wrote Artificial Intelligence: A Modern Approach with Peter Norvig, the textbook that has taught the subject in essentially every university for thirty years. Then spent the later part of his career arguing that optimising a fixed objective is the wrong design, and that systems should be uncertain about what humans want.
card.note: Taught the field its vocabulary, then told it the foundation was wrong.

card.name: Dario Amodei
card.title: Scaling Laws and Anthropic
card.knownFor: Concrete Problems in AI Safety, and the scaling hypothesis
card.scouting: Co-authored Concrete Problems in AI Safety, which gave safety research a concrete agenda, and led the GPT-2 and GPT-3 work where the scaling laws were established. Left OpenAI to co-found Anthropic, whose interpretability and Constitutional AI research is published openly even though the models are not.
card.note: The set’s open-weights sceptic, and its most rigorous public writer on scale.

sources.label: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models (2020)

card.name: Ada Lovelace
card.title: The First Programmer
card.knownFor: Note G, and seeing what the machine could become
card.scouting: Her 1843 notes on Babbage’s Analytical Engine ran three times longer than the paper she was translating and contained Note G, a step-by-step method for computing Bernoulli numbers that is generally read as the first published algorithm. More striking is that she argued the machine could act on things other than numbers, which nobody else did for a century.
card.note: Understood what the machine was for before one had ever been built.

sources.label: Sketch of the Analytical Engine, with Notes (1843)

card.name: Grace Hopper
card.title: Author of the First Compiler
card.knownFor: A-0, COBOL, and machine-independent programming
card.scouting: Wrote the A-0 system in 1952, the first compiler, against a field that told her computers could only do arithmetic. Drove the design of FLOW-MATIC and then COBOL, which put business programming into something close to English and ran the world’s finance for decades. Rear Admiral, and the reason anyone says a program has a bug.
card.note: Argued that code should be readable by humans and won, permanently.

card.name: Margaret Hamilton
card.title: Apollo Guidance Software
card.knownFor: The code that landed Apollo 11, and the phrase software engineering
card.scouting: Led the team that wrote the Apollo onboard flight software at MIT, including the priority scheduling that let the guidance computer shed lower-priority work during the 1202 alarms three minutes before the lunar landing rather than fail. She coined the term software engineering, partly to get the discipline taken seriously.
card.note: The landing happened because her code knew what to drop under load.

card.name: Katherine Johnson
card.title: The Orbital Mathematician
card.knownFor: The trajectory calculations behind Mercury and Apollo
card.scouting: Computed trajectories for Alan Shepard’s flight and the Apollo missions at NASA Langley. When the agency moved to electronic computers for John Glenn’s orbit, Glenn asked for her to check the machine’s numbers by hand before he would fly. Co-authored a 1960 report on orbital calculation, unusual for a woman at Langley then.
card.note: The astronaut trusted her arithmetic over the computer, and he was not wrong to.

card.name: Dorothy Vaughan
card.title: The FORTRAN Supervisor
card.knownFor: Teaching her whole section to program before the machines replaced them
card.scouting: NASA’s first Black supervisor, running the segregated West Area Computing unit. Seeing that the arriving IBM machines would make human computers obsolete, she taught herself FORTRAN and then taught her staff, moving the whole group into programming rather than out of work. That is a rarer kind of technical foresight than the usual sort.
card.note: Saw the automation coming and retrained her entire team ahead of it.

card.name: Jean Bartik
card.title: One of the Six ENIAC Programmers
card.knownFor: Programming the first electronic computer, then teaching it to store programs
card.scouting: One of the six women who programmed ENIAC by physically rewiring it, working from logic diagrams because no programming language or manual existed. They were called operators and left out of the 1946 press photographs. She went on to help convert ENIAC to a stored-program machine and to work on BINAC and UNIVAC.
card.note: Invented the job while doing it, then watched the men be photographed.

card.name: Betty Holberton
card.title: Author of the Sort-Merge Generator
card.knownFor: ENIAC, the first generator program, and readable console design
card.scouting: ENIAC programmer who went on to write the sort-merge generator for UNIVAC, an early instance of a program that writes a program. She argued for the UNIVAC console being grey rather than black on human-factors grounds, worked on the C-10 instruction set, and later contributed to the COBOL and FORTRAN standards.
card.note: Wrote code that wrote code, in 1951, on a machine with mercury memory.

card.name: Kathleen Booth
card.title: Inventor of Assembly Language
card.knownFor: The first assembly language and its assembler
card.scouting: Wrote what is generally considered the first assembly language, for the ARC2 and later APE(X)C machines at Birkbeck, and the assembler to go with it. Co-wrote some of the earliest books on how to program and design these machines, and did early work applying neural network ideas to character recognition in the late 1950s.
card.note: Everything between machine code and a compiler starts here.

card.name: Mary Allen Wilkes
card.title: The First Home Computer User
card.knownFor: The LINC operating system, written in her parents’ living room
card.scouting: Wrote LAP6, the operating system for the LINC, one of the first interactive personal computers. In 1965 she took a LINC home and used it there, which makes her plausibly the first person to have a computer in their house. LAP6 supported real-time text editing on a machine with two kilowords of memory.
card.note: Had a computer at home a decade before anyone was selling one.

card.name: Erna Schneider Hoover
card.title: The Telephone Switch That Stopped Failing
card.knownFor: Computerised call switching under load
card.scouting: At Bell Labs she designed a computerised switching system that monitored incoming call rates and prioritised work to stop exchanges collapsing under peak load, holding one of the first software patents for it. She reportedly sketched the design while in hospital after giving birth, and became the first woman supervisor of a technical department there.
card.note: Solved overload in telephony before anyone called it backpressure.

card.name: Elizabeth Feinler
card.title: Keeper of the Early Internet
card.knownFor: The ARPANET directory, and the top-level domains
card.scouting: Ran the Network Information Center at SRI, which was the ARPANET’s directory, help desk and registry, publishing the Resource Handbook and maintaining the HOSTS.TXT file that every machine on the network relied on. Her group proposed the domain naming scheme that gave us .com, .edu, .gov, .mil, .net and .org.
card.note: Ran the internet’s address book by hand, and named the neighbourhoods.

card.name: Stephanie Shirley
card.title: Founder of Freelance Programmers
card.knownFor: A software house staffed by women working from home, in 1962
card.scouting: Founded Freelance Programmers with six pounds, staffing it almost entirely with women programming from home around their children, decades before remote work had a name. Signed her business letters Steve because Stephanie was not getting replies. The company wrote the Concorde black box flight recorder software and she later gave much of her wealth away.
card.note: Built the case for remote work in 1962 and shipped Concorde’s black box.

card.name: Joan Clarke
card.title: Cryptanalyst, Hut 8
card.knownFor: Breaking naval Enigma at Bletchley Park
card.scouting: One of the very few women doing cryptanalytic rather than clerical work at Bletchley Park, in the Hut 8 team attacking naval Enigma, and a practitioner of Banburismus. She was initially classified as a linguist because the pay grades had no category for a woman cryptanalyst. The work stayed secret for decades, so the record of it is thinner than it should be.
card.note: The openness score is low because the Official Secrets Act made it so.

card.name: Elizebeth Smith Friedman
card.title: The Codebreaker Nobody Credited
card.knownFor: Breaking smuggler and Nazi spy ciphers, then watching Hoover take the credit
card.scouting: Broke the ciphers of rum-runners during Prohibition and testified about it in court, then during the war ran the unit that broke the Enigma traffic of a Nazi spy ring in South America. The FBI publicly claimed those results. Her files stayed classified until 2008, which is why her husband William is the famous Friedman.
card.note: Her work was credited to J. Edgar Hoover for sixty years.

card.name: Hedy Lamarr
card.title: Frequency Hopping
card.knownFor: A wartime patent that anticipated spread spectrum
card.scouting: With composer George Antheil, patented a frequency-hopping scheme in 1942 to stop radio-guided torpedoes being jammed, synchronised by a mechanism borrowed from player pianos. The Navy shelved it. The underlying idea is an ancestor of the spread-spectrum techniques used in later secure and wireless communication, and the patent was allowed to lapse unpaid.
card.note: Filed it, gave it to the Navy for free, and got nothing for decades.

card.name: Frances Allen
card.title: The Optimising Compiler
card.knownFor: Program optimisation, and the first Turing Award to a woman
card.scouting: Spent a career at IBM building the theory and practice of compiler optimisation: control flow analysis, data flow analysis, the interprocedural work that every modern compiler still does. Her 1966 paper on program optimisation is foundational. In 2006 she became the first woman to receive the Turing Award, thirty-nine years after the award began.
card.note: Every fast binary you have ever run is downstream of her analyses.

card.name: Barbara Liskov
card.title: The Substitution Principle
card.knownFor: CLU, abstract data types, and the L in SOLID
card.scouting: Designed CLU, which introduced abstract data types, iterators and a serious treatment of exceptions, and which shows up in the ancestry of most modern languages. The Liskov substitution principle is the L in SOLID. Also did foundational work on Byzantine fault tolerance with Miguel Castro. Turing Award, 2008.
card.note: You use her ideas whether or not you have heard the name.

card.name: Shafi Goldwasser
card.title: Zero-Knowledge Proofs
card.knownFor: Proving you know something without revealing it
card.scouting: With Silvio Micali and Charles Rackoff, introduced zero-knowledge interactive proofs, and with Micali the definition of semantic security that made modern encryption provable rather than merely unbroken. Two-time Godel Prize winner and Turing Award, 2012. Every zk-rollup and privacy protocol shipping today is standing on that 1985 paper.
card.note: Formalised the idea of proving a thing without revealing it.

card.name: Karen Spärck Jones
card.title: Inverse Document Frequency
card.knownFor: The weighting that made search work
card.scouting: Her 1972 paper introduced inverse document frequency: rare terms tell you more than common ones. TF-IDF underpinned search engines for thirty years and is still the baseline every ranking system is measured against. She argued throughout her career that computing was too important to be left to men, and said so in those words.
card.note: One weighting function, and search stopped being useless.

sources.label: A statistical interpretation of term specificity (1972)

card.name: Cynthia Dwork
card.title: Differential Privacy
card.knownFor: A formal definition of what privacy loss even means
card.scouting: Co-invented differential privacy, which gave a mathematical definition to the amount of information a data release leaks about any one person, replacing a field of ad-hoc anonymisation that kept being broken. It is now in the US Census, Apple’s telemetry and Google’s. She also co-authored early work on proof-of-work and on algorithmic fairness.
card.note: Turned privacy from a promise into a quantity you can bound.

card.name: Anita Borg
card.title: Founder of Systers
card.knownFor: Building the network, and the conference that carries her name
card.scouting: An OS researcher who built a fault-tolerant Unix and a memory architecture analysis tool, and who in 1987 started Systers, the first email network for women in computing. Co-founded the Grace Hopper Celebration and the Institute for Women and Technology. The conference now draws tens of thousands a year.
card.note: Built the professional network that a generation of the others came through.

card.name: Lynn Conway
card.title: The VLSI Revolution
card.knownFor: Mead-Conway, and making chip design something you could teach
card.scouting: Invented dynamic instruction scheduling at IBM in the 1960s, was fired when she transitioned, and rebuilt her career from scratch. At Xerox PARC she and Carver Mead created the VLSI design methodology and the textbook that let universities teach chip design, then set up MOSIS so students could actually fabricate. Modern semiconductors are organised the way she said they should be.
card.note: Did it twice, the second time after the industry threw her away.

card.name: Sophie Wilson
card.title: Designer of the ARM Instruction Set
card.knownFor: BBC BASIC, and the architecture in every phone on earth
card.scouting: Wrote BBC BASIC, then designed the original ARM instruction set with Steve Furber, a RISC architecture so efficient the first silicon ran on leakage current when its power was accidentally disconnected. There are now more ARM cores in the world than any other processor architecture, by a wide margin. Later designed the FirePath processor at Broadcom.
card.note: The chip in your pocket runs her instruction set. So does the other one.

card.name: Adele Goldberg
card.title: Smalltalk and the Desktop
card.knownFor: The object-oriented environment Apple walked out with
card.scouting: At Xerox PARC she developed Smalltalk-80 with Alan Kay and Dan Ingalls and wrote the books that let anyone else learn it. She objected to demonstrating it to Steve Jobs and was overruled by management; the Macintosh interface followed. Smalltalk is where object-oriented programming and the modern IDE both actually come from.
card.note: Told PARC not to show Jobs the demo. She was right.

card.name: Susan Kare
card.title: The Icons You Grew Up With
card.knownFor: The Macintosh interface, one pixel at a time
card.scouting: Designed the original Macintosh icons, fonts and cursors on graph paper, inventing a visual grammar for direct manipulation that nobody had needed before. The Command key symbol, the trash can, the watch cursor and the Happy Mac are hers. Later did the same work for NeXT, Microsoft and IBM. Her bitmaps are in MoMA.
card.note: Made the computer look friendly, in a 32 by 32 grid.

card.name: Limor Fried
card.title: Founder of Adafruit
card.knownFor: Open hardware as a business that actually works
card.scouting: Founded Adafruit from an MIT dorm room and built it into a substantial manufacturer that publishes its schematics, board files and firmware openly, alongside thousands of free tutorials. Leads CircuitPython, which put a REPL on microcontrollers and made embedded programming approachable. Proved open hardware can be a real company rather than a gesture.
card.note: The openness score is 99 because the schematics ship with the product.

card.name: Mitchell Baker
card.title: The Mozilla Public License
card.knownFor: Keeping Netscape’s code free, and steering Firefox
card.scouting: Wrote the Mozilla Public License and led the Mozilla project through the open-sourcing of Netscape, the years when it looked dead, and the rise of Firefox, which broke Internet Explorer’s monopoly and dragged web standards forward. Chaired the Mozilla Foundation for two decades of arguing that the browser should answer to users.
card.note: The reason there is still a browser engine not owned by an ad company.

card.name: Audrey Tang
card.title: Open Government, Actually Open
card.knownFor: g0v, Perl 6, and running a ministry in public
card.scouting: Worked on Pugs, the first usable Perl 6 implementation, and on Haskell and Perl tooling, then became a central figure in g0v, the Taiwanese civic hacking community that forks government websites into working versions. As Taiwan’s digital minister she published transcripts of essentially every meeting she took, and used participatory tooling like vTaiwan on real policy.
card.note: Published the minutes of her own meetings. All of them.

card.name: Karen Sandler
card.title: Software Freedom as a Medical Problem
card.knownFor: The Software Freedom Conservancy, and asking to read her own pacemaker
card.scouting: Executive director of the Software Freedom Conservancy, which provides the legal and financial home for a long list of open source projects and does the unglamorous work of GPL enforcement. A lawyer with a heart condition, she has made the argument for auditable code concrete by asking to see the source of the defibrillator implanted in her chest, and being refused.
card.note: The strongest argument for source access anyone has: her own heart.

card.name: Danese Cooper
card.title: The Open Source Diplomat
card.knownFor: Open source programs at Sun, Intel, PayPal and the Node Foundation
card.scouting: Ran open source at Sun during the OpenSolaris and OpenOffice years, then at Intel, PayPal and Wikimedia, and chaired the Node.js Foundation through the io.js reconciliation. Served on the OSI board. Much of what a corporate open source program office does was invented by her arguing with lawyers, repeatedly, for twenty years.
card.note: Spent two decades translating between engineers and general counsel.

card.name: Allison Randal
card.title: Languages, Foundations and Licences
card.knownFor: Parrot, Perl 6 design, and chairing the OSI
card.scouting: Led the Parrot virtual machine and worked on the Perl 6 design, then served as president of the Perl Foundation, chair of the Open Source Initiative, on the board of the Python Software Foundation, and at Canonical and HP on OpenStack. One of the few people equally credible on a language runtime and on licence text.
card.note: Turns up wherever open source needs both a compiler and a constitution.

card.name: Valerie Aurora
card.title: Filesystems and the Ada Initiative
card.knownFor: Linux filesystem work, then changing how conferences behave
card.scouting: Worked on Linux filesystems including ext4, ChunkFS and union mounts, and wrote a long-running series on filesystem design for LWN. Co-founded the Ada Initiative, whose example anti-harassment policy was adopted across a large part of the conference circuit and materially changed what open source events tolerate.
card.note: Shipped kernel code, then fixed the conferences that ran on it.

card.name: Coraline Ada Ehmke
card.title: Author of the Contributor Covenant
card.knownFor: The code of conduct most projects actually use
card.scouting: Wrote the Contributor Covenant in 2014; it has since been adopted by well over a hundred thousand projects including Linux, Rails and Kubernetes, and it is the reason most repositories have a CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md at all. Also created the Hippocratic License and the Organization for Ethical Source, and took a great deal of abuse for both.
card.note: That file in the root of your repo is hers.

card.name: Sumana Harihareswara
card.title: Maintainer of the Maintainers
card.knownFor: pip’s resolver, PyPI funding, and taking project management seriously
card.scouting: Led the successful grant-funded work to replace pip’s dependency resolver, a change every Python user benefits from and almost nobody noticed. Has worked on Wikimedia engineering community, Zulip and MediaWiki, and writes seriously about the unglamorous parts of open source: release management, funding, and how maintainers burn out.
card.note: Fixed pip’s resolver. Consider what your builds were like before.

card.name: Latanya Sweeney
card.title: Re-identification, and k-Anonymity
card.knownFor: Proving anonymised data is not anonymous
card.scouting: Showed that 87 percent of Americans could be uniquely identified from ZIP code, birth date and sex, then demonstrated it by re-identifying the Massachusetts governor’s medical records in a public dataset and mailing them to him. Proposed k-anonymity in response. Later served as chief technologist at the FTC and published work on discrimination in online ad delivery.
card.note: Mailed the governor his own supposedly anonymous health records.

card.name: Jessica McKellar
card.title: Python, and Who Gets to Join
card.knownFor: CPython contributions and PSF leadership
card.scouting: CPython contributor, Python Software Foundation director and Twisted maintainer who did a large amount of the outreach work that widened who shows up to Python: Boston Python’s beginner workshops moved the local user group to roughly a third women, which nobody had managed before. Co-wrote a book on Twisted and taught a great deal for free.
card.note: Ran the workshops that changed who was in the room.

card.name: Carol Willing
card.title: Jupyter and CPython
card.knownFor: The notebook infrastructure science runs on
card.scouting: Project Jupyter steering council member and CPython core developer who has done a great deal of the work on JupyterHub and Binder, the pieces that turn a notebook from a file on someone’s laptop into shared, reproducible infrastructure. Served as a Python Steering Council member and does the release and mentoring work that keeps both projects running.
card.note: Notebooks are how science ships now, and she maintains them.

card.name: Julia Evans
card.title: The Zines
card.knownFor: Explaining systems programming so people actually understand it
card.scouting: Writes hand-drawn zines and a long-running blog that explain strace, tcpdump, DNS, containers, git internals and networking better than the manuals do, mostly by working through her own confusion in public. Wrote a Ruby profiler and various debugging tools. An enormous number of engineers learned how their machine works from her drawings.
card.note: Made "I do not understand this yet" a legitimate way to write documentation.

card.name: Rachel Andrew
card.title: CSS Grid, Explained
card.knownFor: Getting the web to actually use its layout system
card.scouting: CSS Working Group invited expert and the person who did more than anyone to get CSS Grid understood and adopted, through Grid by Example, years of writing and a great deal of patient explanation. Later editor in chief of Smashing Magazine and now on the Chrome developer relations team writing the platform documentation.
card.note: A spec nobody understands is a spec nobody ships. She fixed that.

card.name: Jen Simmons
card.title: Layout on the Real Web
card.knownFor: Intrinsic web design, and shipping CSS in Safari
card.scouting: Coined intrinsic web design for the layout approach Grid and Flexbox actually enable, and spent years demonstrating it in public so designers would stop rebuilding 2010 in a modern browser. Worked on Firefox developer tools including the Grid inspector, and is now an Apple evangelist and CSS Working Group member shipping the features in Safari.
card.note: Argued the web should stop imitating print, then shipped the tools.

card.name: Lea Verou
card.title: CSS, and the Tools Around It
card.knownFor: Prism, Mavo, and CSS Working Group membership
card.scouting: Wrote Prism, the syntax highlighter running on a very large share of technical sites, and a run of small widely-used libraries. CSS Working Group invited expert who has driven several specs including colour functions, wrote CSS Secrets, and researches end-user programming at MIT. Nearly everything she makes is MIT licensed and on GitHub.
card.note: The code highlighting on the docs you read this morning is probably hers.

card.name: Sarah Drasner
card.title: Animation, Vue and Developer Experience
card.knownFor: Vue core team, SVG animation, and leading platform teams
card.scouting: Vue core team member who wrote much of the animation documentation and a well-regarded book on SVG animation, then led developer experience at Netlify, Google and Azure. Her writing on animation performance and on running engineering teams is widely read, and she has published a large amount of demo code for free.
card.note: Made web animation a craft with technique rather than a pile of tricks.

card.name: Léonie Watson
card.title: Accessibility in the Standards
card.knownFor: W3C board, and making the platform work with a screen reader
card.scouting: A blind engineer who has served on the W3C Board of Directors, co-chaired the Web Applications Working Group and worked on the accessibility of HTML, ARIA and the Web Audio API from inside the specs rather than filing bugs from outside. Runs TetraLogical and has spent years teaching developers what their markup actually sounds like.
card.note: Fixed accessibility where it is cheapest to fix: in the spec.

card.name: Charity Majors
card.title: Observability, and Testing in Production
card.knownFor: Honeycomb, and the argument about unknown unknowns
card.scouting: Co-founded Honeycomb and made the case that dashboards of pre-aggregated metrics cannot answer questions you did not think to ask, which reframed monitoring into observability and high-cardinality events. Co-wrote Observability Engineering and Database Reliability Engineering, and has been relentlessly, usefully rude about the idea that you can avoid testing in production.
card.note: You do test in production. She just wants you to admit it and instrument it.

card.name: Liz Fong-Jones
card.title: SRE in the Open
card.knownFor: Site reliability practice, OpenTelemetry advocacy, and organising
card.scouting: Was a Google SRE for over a decade, then principal developer advocate at Honeycomb, pushing OpenTelemetry and publishing a great deal on SLOs and reliability practice that teams actually adopt. Also one of the more visible organisers in the tech worker movement, which cost her something and which she has been candid about.
card.note: Publishes the reliability practice most companies keep as tribal knowledge.

card.name: Jessie Frazelle
card.title: Containers, and Then Silicon
card.knownFor: Docker maintainer, container security, and Oxide
card.scouting: A core Docker maintainer during the years containers took over, known for running absolutely everything in one including desktop applications, and for the seccomp and AppArmor work on container isolation. Later worked on Kubernetes and GitHub, then co-founded Oxide Computer to build servers with an open firmware stack, which is a much harder version of the same argument.
card.note: Containerised her own desktop to prove a point, then went after firmware.

card.name: Camille Fournier
card.title: ZooKeeper, and The Manager’s Path
card.knownFor: Distributed coordination, then teaching engineers to lead
card.scouting: Apache ZooKeeper committer and project chair, and CTO of Rent the Runway, then head of platform engineering at Two Sigma. Wrote The Manager’s Path, which is the book most engineers are handed when they first lead a team, and which is unusually honest about the parts of the job that are not fun.
card.note: Shipped the coordination service, then documented the harder job.

card.name: Timnit Gebru
card.title: Stochastic Parrots
card.knownFor: The paper Google fired her over, and DAIR
card.scouting: Co-authored Gender Shades with Joy Buolamwini, measuring commercial face recognition error rates that reached 34 percent for darker-skinned women against near zero for lighter-skinned men, which forced public changes from IBM and Microsoft. Co-led Google’s ethical AI team until her exit over the Stochastic Parrots paper, then founded DAIR to do the research outside a company.
card.note: The exit made the news. The measurements are why the paper mattered.

card.name: Joy Buolamwini
card.title: Gender Shades
card.knownFor: Auditing face recognition, and being invisible to it
card.scouting: Found as an MIT student that face detection would not see her face until she put on a white mask, and turned that into Gender Shades, a systematic audit of commercial classifiers by skin tone and gender. Founded the Algorithmic Justice League. The work fed directly into moratoria on police use of face recognition in several US cities.
card.note: Started with a white mask in a lab and ended in city legislation.

card.name: Margaret Mitchell
card.title: Model Cards
card.knownFor: Documentation standards for models, and refusing to stop asking
card.scouting: Founded and co-led Google’s ethical AI team, and first-authored Model Cards for Model Reporting, which proposed that a released model should ship with a document stating its intended use, its evaluation data and where it performs worse. Hugging Face made model cards a default. She was fired alongside Gebru and is now chief ethics scientist at Hugging Face.
card.note: Every model card on the Hub traces back to one 2019 paper.

card.name: David Packard
card.title: Co-founder and CEO, Hewlett-Packard
card.knownFor: The garage, and the management doctrine that came out of it
card.scouting: Started HP in a Palo Alto garage in 1939 with Bill Hewlett and $538, and grew it into the template every Valley company copied: engineers running engineering, profit sharing, and an across-the-board pay cut rather than layoffs in a downturn. He set the practice down late in life as The HP Way. The garage is now a California historical landmark.
card.note: Invented the Silicon Valley company before there was a Silicon Valley to put it in.

card.name: Akio Morita
card.title: Co-founder and CEO, Sony
card.knownFor: Making Japanese electronics the thing to beat
card.scouting: Co-founded Sony in the ruins of postwar Tokyo and spent forty years insisting a Japanese company could sell to the world under its own name rather than someone else’s label. Pushed the transistor radio, the Trinitron and, over his own engineers’ objections, the Walkman, a tape player with no record function that sold hundreds of millions. He also lost the format war with Betamax.
card.note: Proved a hardware brand could be built on taste rather than price.

card.name: Thomas J. Watson Jr.
card.title: President and CEO, IBM
card.knownFor: Betting the company on the System/360
card.scouting: Took over his father’s punched-card company and moved it into electronic computing over considerable internal objection. The System/360, announced in 1964 after a development effort usually costed at around $5 billion, was the bet: one architecture spanning the whole product line, so a customer’s software survived the next hardware purchase. Backwards compatibility as a commercial strategy starts here, and mainframes running 360-descended code are still in production sixty years later.
card.note: The most expensive product decision anyone in computing had made, and it worked.

card.name: Ken Olsen
card.title: Founder and President, Digital Equipment Corporation
card.knownFor: The minicomputer, and the machines Unix was written on
card.scouting: Founded DEC in 1957 and built computers people could put their hands on, at a time when a computer meant a room you booked time in. The PDP-7 and PDP-11 are where Unix and C were written; the VAX and VMS ran a generation of university and research computing. He also spent the 1980s dismissing the personal computer, and DEC was sold to Compaq six years after he left.
card.note: Every Unix story starts on one of his machines. The PC story ended his company.

card.name: Robert Noyce
card.title: Co-founder and CEO, Intel
card.knownFor: The integrated circuit, then the company that mass-produced it
card.scouting: Co-invented the silicon integrated circuit at Fairchild, independently of Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments, then co-founded Intel with Gordon Moore in 1968 to build memory and, later, microprocessors. He ran it with the open-plan, no-reserved-parking informality that became the industry’s house style. He was called the Mayor of Silicon Valley, and the eight who walked out of Shockley Semiconductor with him seeded most of what followed.
card.note: Half the companies in the Valley trace their org chart back to his.

card.name: Gordon Moore
card.title: Co-founder and CEO, Intel
card.knownFor: The observation the whole industry then had to keep true
card.scouting: Wrote a short article for Electronics magazine in 1965 noting that the number of components on a chip had been doubling on a regular cadence and would keep doing so. Moore’s law was a market observation that turned into a roadmap the semiconductor industry then organised itself around, decade after decade. He was Intel’s CEO from 1975 to 1987, through the period that made the microprocessor the company’s business.
card.note: The one forecast in tech that firms spent sixty years and trillions of dollars making come true.

card.name: Bill Gates
card.title: Co-founder and CEO, Microsoft
card.knownFor: Software as a licensed product, on every desk
card.scouting: Understood before anyone that the money was in the software, not the machine, and structured the 1980 MS-DOS deal with IBM to keep the right to license it to everybody else. His 1976 Open Letter to Hobbyists, which called copying Altair BASIC theft, is the document free software spent twenty years arguing with. Microsoft was found to have violated the Sherman Act in 2000.
card.note: The counterparty in the argument this entire site descends from.

card.name: Steve Jobs
card.title: Co-founder and CEO, Apple
card.knownFor: Apple twice, NeXT, Pixar, and the phone
card.scouting: Co-founded Apple in 1976, was forced out in 1985, founded NeXT, bought Pixar, and returned in 1997 to a company close to insolvency. What came back with him mattered technically as well as commercially: NeXTSTEP became macOS and iOS, putting a BSD-derived Unix under hundreds of millions of consumer machines, and Apple’s KHTML fork became WebKit. The iPhone reset what a computer is.
card.note: Ran the most valuable company on earth on taste, and got away with it.

card.name: Larry Ellison
card.title: Co-founder and CEO, Oracle
card.knownFor: Selling the relational database to the enterprise
card.scouting: Read Codd’s paper on the relational model and shipped a commercial product from it before IBM did, then spent thirty-seven years as CEO making Oracle the enterprise system of record, largely by acquisition: PeopleSoft, Siebel, and in 2010 Sun. That made Oracle the steward of Java and MySQL, and the plaintiff in Google v. Oracle. The Supreme Court ruled fair use in 2021.
card.note: Owns more of the software you depend on than the licence file admits.

sources.label: Google LLC v. Oracle America, Inc.

card.name: N. R. Narayana Murthy
card.title: Co-founder and CEO, Infosys
card.knownFor: Building the Indian software industry as an export business
card.scouting: Founded Infosys in 1981 with six colleagues and seed money borrowed from his wife, and built it into the company that made offshore software delivery a credible global business rather than a cost-cutting rumour. Infosys became the first India-registered company listed on Nasdaq, in 1999. Domestically he was as known for insisting on Western-standard disclosure and governance at a time when neither was expected of an Indian firm.
card.note: Rewired where the world’s software gets written, without writing much of it himself.

card.name: Masayoshi Son
card.title: Founder and CEO, SoftBank
card.knownFor: The largest technology bets ever placed, in both directions
card.scouting: Built SoftBank from software distribution into a telecoms operator and then the most consequential technology investor alive. An early stake in Alibaba, bought for around $20 million, returned tens of billions. He acquired Arm, whose instruction set is in essentially every phone on earth, for about $32 billion in 2016, and launched the $100 billion Vision Fund, which then produced WeWork.
card.note: Nobody has been spectacularly right and spectacularly wrong at this scale.

card.name: Michael Dell
card.title: Founder and CEO, Dell
card.knownFor: Build to order, and the largest tech buyout of its time
card.scouting: Started assembling PCs in a University of Texas dorm room in 1984 and turned direct sales and negative working capital into a manufacturing weapon: the customer paid before the supplier did. He took the company private in a $24.4 billion buyout in 2013, then bought EMC, and with it VMware, for about $67 billion in 2016.
card.note: The supply chain was the product. Everything else was a box.

card.name: Scott McNealy
card.title: Co-founder and CEO, Sun Microsystems
card.knownFor: The network is the computer, and giving Java away
card.scouting: Ran Sun for twenty-two years and shipped an extraordinary amount of what the internet was built on: NFS, SPARC, Solaris and Java. Sun published NFS as an open specification, released OpenSolaris in 2005 and put Java under the GPL in 2006, decisions that outlived the company since OpenJDK is what most Java runs on today. Commodity Linux boxes killed the workstation business.
card.note: Gave away more load-bearing software than any CEO before him, and still lost the company.

card.name: Morris Chang
card.title: Founder and CEO, TSMC
card.knownFor: Inventing the pure-play foundry, and with it the fabless industry
card.scouting: Spent twenty-five years at Texas Instruments, then founded TSMC in 1987 on a proposition nobody had tried: a chip factory that designs nothing of its own and therefore never competes with its customers. That decision is why a company can exist with brilliant chip designers and no fab, which is to say why Nvidia, AMD and Apple Silicon exist in their current form.
card.note: Changed the shape of an entire industry by choosing what not to build.

card.name: Andrew Grove
card.title: CEO, Intel
card.knownFor: The memory-to-microprocessor pivot, and the management text about it
card.scouting: Escaped Hungary in 1956, joined Intel as its first hire, and as CEO from 1987 to 1998 pushed the company out of the memory business it was founded on and into microprocessors, after Japanese competitors made DRAM unprofitable. He wrote the discipline up in High Output Management and Only the Paranoid Survive. Intel’s revenue grew roughly tenfold on his watch.
card.note: Killed his own company’s founding product before somebody else did.

card.name: Ren Zhengfei
card.title: Founder and CEO, Huawei
card.knownFor: The world’s largest telecom equipment maker, and the sanctions fight
card.scouting: Founded Huawei in Shenzhen in 1987 reselling telephone switches, and built the largest supplier of telecommunications equipment on earth. US restrictions from 2019 cut the company off from advanced chips and Google’s Android services, and the response was to fund substitutes in the open: HarmonyOS, and openEuler and openGauss handed to a Chinese open source foundation.
card.note: Carded for scale and for what being cut off made the company release.

card.name: Lou Gerstner
card.title: Chairman and CEO, IBM
card.knownFor: Turning IBM around, and putting a billion dollars behind Linux
card.scouting: Arrived from RJR Nabisco in 1993 at an IBM losing billions and widely expected to be broken up, kept it whole, and pivoted it from hardware to services. The decision that matters here was announced in 2000: roughly a billion dollars of IBM investment into Linux, plus lawyers and patent cover. Nothing did more to make Linux acceptable in enterprise procurement.
card.note: The suit who made Linux safe to buy.

card.name: Jensen Huang
card.title: Co-founder and CEO, Nvidia
card.knownFor: CUDA, and the hardware the entire AI industry runs on
card.scouting: Co-founded Nvidia in 1993 to build graphics chips for games, then funded CUDA, a way to run general computation on them, long before there was a market for it. When deep learning arrived, the hardware and the programming model were already there. The open source relationship is two-sided: the proprietary Linux driver drew Torvalds’ famous 2012 insult, and the kernel modules were opened in 2022.
card.note: Spent a decade funding a bet on a market that did not exist yet.

card.name: Bob Young
card.title: Co-founder and CEO, Red Hat
card.knownFor: Proving you can build a real business on software you give away
card.scouting: Sold Linux CDs out of a catalogue business, co-founded Red Hat with Marc Ewing, and worked out the argument that made open source investable: nobody pays for the bits, they pay for support, certification and someone to call. Red Hat’s 1999 IPO was one of the largest first-day gains in Nasdaq history, and the moment Wall Street conceded free software was a business.
card.note: The business model half of open source has one author, and it is him.

card.name: Jeff Bezos
card.title: Founder and CEO, Amazon
card.knownFor: Retail, then renting the internet its computers
card.scouting: Started an online bookshop in 1994 and ran it for twenty-seven years on deliberately thin margins and reinvestment, which is how it outlasted competitors optimising for quarterly profit. The decision with the deepest technical consequences was internal: an API mandate that every team expose its data over service interfaces, which turned Amazon’s own plumbing into AWS in 2006.
card.note: Sold books until the warehouse for the internet turned out to be the business.

card.name: Reed Hastings
card.title: Co-founder and CEO, Netflix
card.knownFor: Cannibalising his own business twice, on purpose
card.scouting: Co-founded Netflix as a DVD-by-post service in 1997, launched streaming in 2007 against his own profitable business, then commissioned originals against the studios he licensed from. Netflix engineering shaped how the industry runs services at scale and published most of it: Chaos Monkey, Hystrix, Eureka and Zuul all shipped as open source, and chaos engineering came out of that work.
card.note: Broke his own company twice before anyone else could.

card.name: Meg Whitman
card.title: CEO, eBay and Hewlett-Packard
card.knownFor: Scaling the first great internet marketplace
card.scouting: Joined eBay in 1998 when it had a few dozen employees and left in 2008 with tens of thousands, having turned an auction site into proof that strangers would transact online at scale, and having bought PayPal in 2002, which mattered more to the internet than the auctions did. She later ran HP through its split into HP Inc and HPE.
card.note: Made online payment between strangers normal, which everything after assumes.

card.name: Diane Greene
card.title: Co-founder and CEO, VMware
card.knownFor: Making virtualisation work on commodity x86
card.scouting: Co-founded VMware in 1998 and ran it for a decade, shipping the thing everyone had been told was impractical: efficient virtualisation of an x86 architecture never designed for it. The consequence is the modern data centre. Server consolidation, live migration and the economics that made public cloud viable all rest on that work. She later ran Google Cloud.
card.note: Every cloud instance you have ever rented is downstream of her company’s hypervisor.

card.name: Larry Page
card.title: Co-founder and CEO, Google and Alphabet
card.knownFor: PageRank, then giving away the mobile operating system
card.scouting: Co-invented PageRank as a Stanford graduate student and co-founded Google in 1998, serving as CEO twice. Two decisions on his watch had enormous open source consequence: Android was released permissively and given to handset makers, which is why most phones run a Linux kernel, and Chromium was open-sourced, which is why nearly every non-Safari browser is a Chromium derivative.
card.note: The most consequential giving-away of code by a company that was not trying to be an open source company.

card.name: Marc Benioff
card.title: Founder and CEO, Salesforce
card.knownFor: The End of Software, and the subscription model that replaced it
card.scouting: Left Oracle to found Salesforce in 1999 behind a marketing campaign built on a red circle struck through the word Software, and made multi-tenant applications delivered over a browser the default way businesses buy anything. Almost every enterprise product now sold by subscription, including most open source companies’ commercial tiers, operates in the category he legitimised.
card.note: Invented the pricing page the rest of the industry now uses.

card.name: Jack Ma
card.title: Founder and CEO, Alibaba
card.knownFor: Building China’s commerce infrastructure from an apartment
card.scouting: A former English teacher who founded Alibaba in his Hangzhou apartment in 1999, beat eBay in China with Taobao, and solved the trust problem with an escrow payment system that became Alipay. Alibaba’s 2014 New York listing raised about $25 billion, the largest IPO in history at the time. Dubbo and RocketMQ are Apache projects that came out of the company.
card.note: The card that shows how much of the internet was built outside Silicon Valley.

card.name: Mårten Mickos
card.title: CEO, MySQL AB
card.knownFor: The billion-dollar exit that made open core a category
card.scouting: Ran MySQL AB from 2001 and sold it to Sun in 2008 for about a billion dollars, the most anyone had paid for an open source company. MySQL was the M in LAMP, so the deal proved a freely licensed database with a paid support tier could be worth as much as a proprietary one. He later ran Eucalyptus and HackerOne.
card.note: The exit every open source founder cited for the following decade.

card.name: Eric Schmidt
card.title: CEO, Google; previously CEO, Novell
card.knownFor: Turning a research culture into an operating company
card.scouting: Worked on Unix tooling early, was CTO at Sun during the Java years and CEO of Novell, then ran Google from 2001 to 2011, hired as adult supervision for two founders in their twenties. He built the advertising machine and the management structure that carried the company from a few hundred people to tens of thousands, and presided over the Android and YouTube acquisitions.
card.note: Three of the companies on this card list are places he ran or nearly did.

card.name: Mark Zuckerberg
card.title: Founder and CEO, Meta
card.knownFor: Three billion users, React, PyTorch and open-weight models
card.scouting: Founded Facebook in a Harvard dorm in 2004 and still runs the company two decades and about three billion users later, through Cambridge Analytica, the Instagram and WhatsApp deals, and the pivot to Meta. The open source record is enormous and largely separate from the reputational one: React, PyTorch, GraphQL, RocksDB, the Open Compute Project, and the Llama open-weight models.
card.note: The most-criticised CEO in tech also runs its largest open source operation.

card.name: Tobias Lütke
card.title: Founder and CEO, Shopify
card.knownFor: A Rails core contributor who kept the company on Rails
card.scouting: Tried to sell snowboards online in 2004, found the available software unusable, and wrote his own in Ruby on Rails, early enough that he became a Rails core contributor while doing it. Shopify grew into the platform behind millions of storefronts and remains one of the largest Ruby deployments anywhere, with Liquid, its templating language, released as open source.
card.note: The rare public-company CEO whose GitHub profile is not decorative.

card.name: Elon Musk
card.title: CEO, Tesla, SpaceX and X
card.knownFor: Rockets, electric cars, and releasing the patents
card.scouting: Runs several companies at once and has changed at least two industries: SpaceX made orbital launch reusable and drove cost per kilogram down by an order of magnitude, and Tesla made electric cars something people wanted rather than tolerated. In 2014 Tesla pledged not to enforce its patents against anyone using them in good faith. He bought Twitter for $44 billion in 2022.
card.note: Carded for the launch cost curve and the patent pledge, not the posting.

card.name: Daniel Ek
card.title: Co-founder and CEO, Spotify
card.knownFor: Making streaming better than piracy
card.scouting: Co-founded Spotify in Stockholm in 2006 with an engineering goal that sounds trivial and was not: a track had to start playing faster than a pirated file on your own disk. The early peer-to-peer work solved it, and the licensing deals dragged the record industry into a model it had spent a decade litigating against. Spotify also gave the industry Backstage.
card.note: Beat piracy on latency, which is a more honest explanation than the marketing.

card.name: Andy Jassy
card.title: Founder of AWS; CEO, Amazon
card.knownFor: Building the cloud, and the licence backlash it caused
card.scouting: Wrote the original business plan for what became AWS and ran it from 2006 until succeeding Bezos in 2021. AWS turned computing into a utility. It also set off the defining licensing fight of the era: Elastic, MongoDB and Redis changed licences over managed services built on their code, and Amazon forked Elasticsearch into OpenSearch, later donated to the Linux Foundation.
card.note: The reason the SSPL exists, and the reason OpenSearch does.

card.name: Chris Wanstrath
card.title: Co-founder and CEO, GitHub
card.knownFor: The place the world’s open source moved to
card.scouting: Co-founded GitHub in 2008 and was CEO through the period when it became the default home of open source, largely by making the pull request a social object rather than a mailing-list patch. The company was bootstrapped for four years, ran on a famously flat structure that later came apart, and sold to Microsoft for $7.5 billion in 2018.
card.note: Turned reviewing a patch into something people do for fun.

card.name: Jim Whitehurst
card.title: CEO, Red Hat
card.knownFor: Taking an open source company past three billion in revenue
card.scouting: Came from Delta Air Lines to run Red Hat in 2008 and grew it from about $500 million to over $3 billion in annual revenue, the first open source company at that scale, before selling to IBM for $34 billion in 2019. He wrote The Open Organization, and backed the OpenShift bet on Kubernetes early.
card.note: The proof that the open source business model scales past the true believers.

card.name: Matthew Prince
card.title: Co-founder and CEO, Cloudflare
card.knownFor: A free tier that quietly became internet infrastructure
card.scouting: Co-founded Cloudflare in 2009 with Michelle Zatlyn and Lee Holloway and gave away DDoS protection and a CDN to anyone who asked, which is why a large share of the web now passes through it. The company open-sourced Quiche, Pingora and the Workers runtime, funded Let’s Encrypt, and runs Project Galileo for civil society sites at no charge.
card.note: Gave away the expensive part and made the internet structurally dependent on it.

card.name: Patrick Collison
card.title: Co-founder and CEO, Stripe
card.knownFor: Seven lines of code instead of a merchant account
card.scouting: Founded Stripe with his brother John in 2010, when accepting a card online meant weeks of paperwork with a bank, and replaced it with an API you could integrate in an afternoon. The company set the standard for what developer documentation is expected to look like, and open-sourced Sorbet, a gradual type checker for Ruby now used well beyond Stripe.
card.note: Made the payments industry answer to developers rather than procurement.

card.name: Tim Cook
card.title: CEO, Apple
card.knownFor: Operating the largest company in the world, and Swift
card.scouting: Joined Apple in 1998 and rebuilt its supply chain into the most efficient operation in consumer electronics, then took over in 2011 and grew the company past a three trillion dollar valuation. The move to Apple Silicon was the largest architecture migration any consumer platform has attempted. Apple open-sourced Swift in 2015 and funds LLVM, Clang and WebKit.
card.note: The logistics person who turned out to be the right kind of successor.

card.name: Ginni Rometty
card.title: Chairman and CEO, IBM
card.knownFor: Buying Red Hat for thirty-four billion dollars
card.scouting: Joined IBM as a systems engineer in 1981 and became its first woman CEO in 2012, running the company through a long and contested revenue decline as it shifted toward cloud. The decision she will be remembered for is the 2019 acquisition of Red Hat for $34 billion, structured to leave Red Hat operating independently, which is why the community did not scatter.
card.note: Paid the largest sum in software history for a company that gives its product away.

card.name: Pat Gelsinger
card.title: CEO, VMware and Intel
card.knownFor: An 80486 architect who came back to run the company
card.scouting: Joined Intel at eighteen, led the design of the 80486 and became the company’s first CTO, then ran VMware from 2012 through its Kubernetes pivot, then returned as Intel’s CEO in 2021 to attempt the hardest turnaround in the industry: rebuilding leading-edge manufacturing against TSMC. He left in 2024 with that unfinished.
card.note: The engineer’s engineer handed the hardest job in semiconductors, twenty years late.

card.name: Satya Nadella
card.title: CEO, Microsoft
card.knownFor: Microsoft loves Linux, and meaning it
card.scouting: Took over Microsoft in 2014, a company whose previous CEO had called Linux a cancer, and reversed the posture completely: .NET open-sourced and cross-platform, the Linux kernel shipped inside Windows as WSL, VS Code released under MIT, Microsoft joining the Linux Foundation, and GitHub bought for $7.5 billion in 2018 and left to run itself.
card.note: Turned the villain of Series One’s founding argument into the largest corporate contributor to open source.

card.name: Lisa Su
card.title: CEO, AMD
card.knownFor: The turnaround that put competition back into x86
card.scouting: An MIT-trained semiconductor engineer with real silicon credentials, she took over an AMD near collapse in 2014, bet everything on the Zen architecture and a chiplet strategy, and turned it into a company that took server share from Intel and grew its market value more than fiftyfold. AMD’s ROCm stack is open source, the only credible open alternative to CUDA.
card.note: The most complete corporate turnaround in modern hardware, run by someone who could read the layouts.

card.name: Susan Wojcicki
card.title: CEO, YouTube
card.knownFor: The garage, AdSense, and the royalty-free video codecs
card.scouting: Rented her Menlo Park garage to Google’s founders in 1998, became employee sixteen, built AdSense into the business that funded the free web, argued for buying YouTube in 2006, and ran it from 2014 to 2023. The open thread runs through the codecs: Google released VP8 and VP9 royalty-free, then AV1 through the Alliance for Open Media. She died in 2024.
card.note: Ran the platform, and quietly made its file format free for everyone else.

card.name: Sid Sijbrandij
card.title: Co-founder and CEO, GitLab
card.knownFor: Open core, an all-remote company, and a handbook anyone can read
card.scouting: Turned Dmitriy Zaporozhets’ side project into a company in 2012 and took it public in 2021, running one of the few genuinely successful open core businesses: the community edition stays free and self-hostable while the enterprise tiers pay the bills. GitLab has been all-remote from the start and publishes its entire internal handbook in public.
card.note: Runs the company with the doors off, and it is a public company.

card.name: Jay Kreps
card.title: Co-founder and CEO, Confluent
card.knownFor: Writing Kafka, then building the company around it
card.scouting: Co-created Apache Kafka at LinkedIn to solve the company’s own data-pipeline mess, wrote The Log, the essay that taught a generation of engineers to think of state as a replayable stream, and left in 2014 to found Confluent around it. Kafka is now infrastructure at most large companies, and Confluent went public in 2021.
card.note: Wrote the thing, then had to work out how to keep the lights on around it.

card.name: Sundar Pichai
card.title: CEO, Google and Alphabet
card.knownFor: Chrome, Android, and the browser that ate the desktop
card.scouting: Made his name arguing internally that Google should build a browser at all, shipped Chrome in 2008 and took it from nothing to dominant, picking up Android and Chrome OS on the way before becoming CEO in 2015. Google under him released TensorFlow, Kubernetes, Go and Chromium, while facing antitrust rulings over the businesses that pay for all of it.
card.note: Runs the company that both funds and dominates the open web.

card.name: Guillermo Rauch
card.title: Founder and CEO, Vercel
card.knownFor: Next.js, and making deployment a git push
card.scouting: Wrote socket.io and mongoose before founding the company now called Vercel, which maintains Next.js, the most used React framework, and turned preview deployments on every pull request into a baseline expectation rather than a luxury. He is also the clearest example of the open-core tension of his generation: the framework is MIT, the hosting is the business.
card.note: Ships the framework, hosts the framework, and takes the argument about it in public.

card.name: Ali Ghodsi
card.title: Co-founder and CEO, Databricks
card.knownFor: Spark out of a research lab and into every data platform
card.scouting: One of the Berkeley AMPLab researchers behind Apache Spark, which replaced MapReduce as the default way to process large datasets, and CEO of Databricks since 2016. The company has kept releasing the substrate rather than hoarding it: Delta Lake, MLflow, Unity Catalog and the Dolly models were all open-sourced, and it bought MosaicML and Tabular to keep the open table format from fragmenting.
card.note: A professor who turned the lab’s output into a platform without closing the source.

card.name: Nat Friedman
card.title: CEO, GitHub
card.knownFor: Running GitHub after Microsoft bought it, and shipping Copilot
card.scouting: Co-founded Ximian with Miguel de Icaza, carded in Series One, working on GNOME and Mono, then ran GitHub from 2018 to 2021, the years when the community expected Microsoft to ruin it. Instead private repositories became free, Actions and Codespaces shipped, and the Arctic Code Vault buried a snapshot of open source in a Norwegian mine.
card.note: Took over the thing everyone expected to be spoiled, and it was not.

card.name: Sam Altman
card.title: CEO, OpenAI
card.knownFor: ChatGPT, and the argument about what open means
card.scouting: Ran Y Combinator from 2014 to 2019, then OpenAI, where ChatGPT reached a hundred million users faster than any consumer product before it and forced every large technology company to reorganise around one technology. He was fired by his own board in November 2023 and reinstated five days later. The name is the permanent argument: frontier models closed, Whisper and gpt-oss open.
card.note: The most consequential CEO in tech right now, and the one whose company name is a standing dispute.
